concepts.coreInsight: Ibrahim is honored by Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike - he is the common father of faith traditions, embodying submission to the One God.
concepts.whyItMatters: Ibrahim's legacy shows that true faith transcends sectarian boundaries. His example of radical trust in God unites rather than divides.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: ابراہیم کو یہودی، عیسائی اور مسلمان یکساں طور پر عزت دیتے ہیں - وہ ایمانی روایات کے مشترکہ باپ ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ابراہیم کی میراث دکھاتی ہے کہ حقیقی ایمان فرقہ وارانہ حدود سے ماورا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يُكرم إبراهيم من قبل اليهود والمسيحيين والمسلمين - هو الأب المشترك لتقاليد الإيمان.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: إرث إبراهيم يُظهر أن الإيمان الحقيقي يتجاوز الحدود الطائفية.

109.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse records the salutation that Allah preserved for Ibrahim, which Muslims repeat in their prayers. Ibn Kathir explains that this greeting is incorporated into Islamic prayer during the tashahhud, where Muslims ask Allah to bless Muhammad and his family as He blessed Ibrahim and his family. Al-Razi notes that the salutation of peace is particularly fitting for Ibrahim, who became Khalil Allah, the intimate friend of Allah, a station of perfect peace and harmony with the Divine. Tabari records that this greeting has been repeated by believers since the time of the revelation, fulfilling Allah's promise to preserve Ibrahim's honored remembrance. Qurtubi emphasizes that the simplicity of the greeting makes it accessible to all believers, regardless of language or education, ensuring universal participation in honoring Ibrahim. Shia scholars particularly emphasize the connection between this salutation and the one given to the Prophet Muhammad, seeing continuity in how Allah honors His chosen prophets and their families. Sunni commentator al-Baydawi notes that the greeting appears in the Quran itself, giving it special sanctity and ensuring its preservation. Both traditions agree that when believers repeat this salutation, they participate in Allah's honoring of Ibrahim and connect themselves to his legacy of faith and submission.
109.layer4_urdu: سنی اور شیعہ دونوں علماء اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ آیت وہ سلام ریکارڈ کرتی ہے جو اللہ تعالیٰ نے ابراہیم علیہ السلام کے لیے محفوظ رکھا، جسے مسلمان اپنی نمازوں میں دہراتے ہیں۔ ابن کثیر نے وضاحت کی کہ یہ سلام اسلامی نماز میں تشہد کے دوران شامل کیا گیا ہے، جہاں مسلمان اللہ تعالیٰ سے درخواست کرتے ہیں کہ وہ محمد صلی اللہ علیہ وآلہ وسلم اور ان کے خاندان کو برکت دے جیسا کہ اس نے ابراہیم علیہ السلام اور ان کے خاندان کو برکت دی۔ رازی نے نوٹ کیا کہ سلامتی کا سلام خاص طور پر ابراہیم علیہ السلام کے لیے موزوں ہے، جو خلیل اللہ یعنی اللہ کے قریبی دوست بنے، کامل سلامتی کا مقام۔ طبری نے روایات ریکارڈ کیں کہ کس طرح یہ سلام صحابہ کے زمانے سے اسلامی عبادت کا حصہ ہے۔ دونوں روایات اس سلام کو اللہ تعالیٰ اور ابراہیم علیہ السلام کے درمیان خاص تعلق کی علامت کے طور پر دیکھتی ہیں۔
109.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تُسجِّل تحية الله التي خلَّدها لإبراهيم والتي يُرددها المسلمون في صلواتهم. فابن كثير يُبيِّن أن هذه التحية مُدرَجة في التشهد الإسلامي حيث يسأل المسلمون الله أن يُصلِّي على محمد وآله كما صلَّى على إبراهيم وآله. ويُلاحِظ الرازي أن تحية السلام أليق ما يُهدى لإبراهيم لأنه بلغ مقام خليل الله وهو مقام كمال السلام والوئام مع الله. ويُسجِّل الطبري أن هذه التحية يُرددها المؤمنون منذ عهد التنزيل تحقيقاً لوعد الله بحفظ الذكر الحسن. ويُبيِّن القرطبي أن بساطة التحية تجعلها في متناول جميع المؤمنين أياً كانت لغتهم أو ثقافتهم أو مستواهم العلمي مما يكفل المشاركة العالمية في تكريم إبراهيم. ويُشدِّد علماء الشيعة خصوصاً على الصلة بين هذه التحية وتلك المُسبَغة على النبي محمد صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم رائين استمراراً في تكريم الله لأنبيائه المختارين وآلهم الطاهرين. ويُلاحِظ المفسر السني البيضاوي أن التحية وردت في القرآن ذاته مما يمنحها قدسيةً خاصة ويكفل حفظها في الوحي. ويتفق التراثان على أن حين يُردِّد المؤمنون هذه التحية فإنهم يُشاركون في تكريم الله لإبراهيم ويتَّصلون بإرثه العظيم من الإيمان والتسليم.
109.layer1: Verse 109 is a divine proclamation of peace and blessing: 'Peace upon Abraham.' This salutation — Salamun ala Ibrahim — is Allah's own greeting extended to His beloved prophet, acknowledging him with the most honored of salutations. In Arabic, 'salam' carries multiple dimensions: it means peace, safety, wholeness, and freedom from harm. When Allah declares 'salam' upon a prophet or servant, it is the highest possible endorsement and honor that can be bestowed in this world or the next. This verse is particularly moving in its brevity: after describing the monumental trial and the divine ransom, Allah does not add lengthy praise but offers this simple, complete, and eternal greeting. The verse also establishes a pattern that Muslims continue to this day — whenever the name of Ibrahim is mentioned in Islamic contexts, believers add 'alayhi al-salam' (peace be upon him) as an act of continuing Allah's declaration of honor upon him. Furthermore, in every prayer, Muslims recite the Salawat al-Ibrahimiyya which includes asking Allah to send peace and blessings upon Ibrahim. So this divine greeting, first uttered by Allah in this verse, echoes across every salah performed by every Muslim. The verse teaches believers that when a person endures the greatest of trials with sincerity and trust in Allah, the reward is not merely worldly relief but divine honor — to be greeted personally by the Lord of all creation.
109.layer2: Ibn Kathir in his tafsir explains that this verse is the direct divine response to Ibrahim's ordeal — Allah greets him with 'salam' as a sign of approval, acceptance, and divine closeness. Ibn Kathir notes that this salutation appears in the same form for other prophets in Surah as-Saffat, including Nuh (verse 79) and Musa and Harun (verse 120), confirming that it is a specific honor Allah reserves for His prophets who pass the supreme trials assigned to them. Al-Tabari explains that 'salamun ala Ibrahim' functions as a divine proclamation to the entire creation that Ibrahim stands under Allah's special protection and approval. The use of the nominative form 'salamun' (indefinite) rather than the definite 'al-salamu' carries a significance noted by classical Arabic grammarians: the indefinite form implies 'a salam of which the greatness and completeness cannot be fully defined,' suggesting an honor beyond what any specific formulation could capture. Al-Qurtubi connects this verse to the theological principle that the 'salam' of Allah upon His servant is also a form of divine mercy that encompasses both this world and the Hereafter — Ibrahim is safe from disgrace in this life and secure in his status in the life to come. Al-Razi notes that the placement of this divine greeting immediately after the mention of the ransom and before the declaration of reward (verse 110) shows that divine approval is expressed first as an intimate personal greeting before it is elaborated as a system of reward.
109.layer3: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reflects on the depth of this brief verse: after the towering drama of the sacrifice narrative, Allah addresses His intimate friend Ibrahim with a salutation of just three Arabic words — 'salamun ala Ibrahim' — and in those words contains everything: safety, honor, approval, love, and divine closeness. Qutb writes that there is a profound human lesson here, that the greatest acknowledgments of worth are often expressed in simplicity and directness, and that Allah's way of honoring the righteous is through personal, intimate recognition rather than grandiose proclamation. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir highlights that this verse is directly referenced in the prayer formula that Muslims recite — the Salawat al-Ibrahimiyya — which is required in the Tashahhud of every prayer. This means the divine salutation of verse 109 is institutionalized in the five daily prayers of every Muslim, so Ibrahim receives this honor renewed millions of times every day around the world. Contemporary scholars including Sheikh Salih al-Fawzan have noted that the recitation of salawat upon Ibrahim in prayer is not merely historical commemoration but an act of spiritual solidarity — each Muslim joins Allah's own proclamation of honor upon His friend. Ibn Uthaymeen commented that greeting a person with 'salam' in Islam is an act of love and brotherhood, and when Allah uses this greeting for Ibrahim, it reveals the intimacy of their relationship and serves as a model for believers to aspire to — to strive to be people whom Allah greets with His own peace.

concepts.title: Divine Reward
concepts.coreInsight: 'Thus We reward' (kadhalika najzi) establishes a divine pattern - excellence in faith receives excellence in reward, both in this world and the hereafter.
concepts.whyItMatters: Allah's reward system is consistent and just. When we strive for excellence in worship and character, we can trust that Allah will honor our efforts.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'اسی طرح ہم بدلہ دیتے ہیں' ایک الہی نمونہ قائم کرتا ہے - ایمان میں بہترین ہونے کا بدلہ بہترین اجر ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ کا انعام کا نظام مستقل اور منصفانہ ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'كذلك نجزي' يؤسس نمطاً إلهياً - التميز في الإيمان ينال تميزاً في الأجر.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: نظام مكافأة الله ثابت وعادل.

concepts.title: Doers of Good
concepts.coreInsight: 'Al-muhsinin' refers to those who perfect their actions through excellence (ihsan) - doing what's right with beauty, sincerity, and consciousness of Allah.
concepts.whyItMatters: It's not enough to do good; we must do good excellently, as if Allah is watching - because He is. Quality matters as much as quantity in worship.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'محسنین' ان لوگوں کی طرف اشارہ کرتا ہے جو بہترین (احسان) کے ذریعے اپنے اعمال کو کامل کرتے ہیں - خوبصورتی، خلوص اور اللہ کے شعور کے ساتھ صحیح کام کرنا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: نیکی کرنا کافی نہیں ہے؛ ہمیں نیکی بہترین طریقے سے کرنی چاہیے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'المحسنين' يشير إلى أولئك الذين يتقنون أعمالهم من خلال الإحسان - فعل الصواب بجمال وإخلاص.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: لا يكفي أن نفعل الخير؛ يجب أن نفعله بإتقان.

concepts.title: Universal Principle
concepts.coreInsight: This verse isn't just about Ibrahim - it's a timeless principle that applies to all believers who strive for excellence in submission to Allah.
concepts.whyItMatters: Ibrahim's reward shows us our own potential. The same divine system that honored him is available to honor us when we pursue excellence.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: یہ آیت صرف ابراہیم کے بارے میں نہیں ہے - یہ ایک لازوال اصول ہے جو تمام مومنین پر لاگو ہوتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ابراہیم کا اجر ہمیں ہماری اپنی صلاحیت دکھاتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: هذه الآية ليست فقط عن إبراهيم - إنها مبدأ أبدي ينطبق على جميع المؤمنين.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: أجر إبراهيم يُظهر لنا إمكاناتنا الخاصة.

110.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse establishes Allah's consistent principle of rewarding those who excel in faith and righteous action. Ibn Kathir explains that the verse generalizes from Ibrahim's specific example to all believers, encouraging everyone to strive for ihsan. Al-Razi discusses the concept of ihsan extensively, explaining that it involves perfecting one's relationship with Allah, with oneself, and with others, and that such excellence never goes unrewarded. Tabari notes that the verse appears throughout the Quran in similar forms, establishing reward for righteousness as a fundamental divine principle. Qurtubi emphasizes that the reward is both worldly and eternal: good reputation, blessed influence, and ease in this life, plus paradise and divine pleasure in the hereafter. Shia scholars particularly emphasize that the verse invites all believers to emulate Ibrahim's excellence, democratizing spiritual achievement rather than reserving it for prophets. Sunni commentator al-Baydawi explains that 'thus' indicates that Allah's method of rewarding Ibrahim sets the standard for how He rewards all muhsinin. Both traditions agree that ihsan represents the highest level of Islamic practice, going beyond mere obedience to achieve beauty and excellence in all aspects of faith. All schools teach that this verse provides encouragement and hope, affirming that righteous effort is never wasted and that Allah's justice ensures appropriate reward for every good deed.
110.layer4_urdu: سنی اور شیعہ دونوں علماء اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ آیت ایمان اور نیک عمل میں بہترین حاصل کرنے والوں کو انعام دینے کا اللہ تعالیٰ کا مستقل اصول قائم کرتی ہے۔ ابن کثیر نے وضاحت کی کہ آیت ابراہیم علیہ السلام کی مخصوص مثال سے تمام مومنوں تک عام کرتی ہے، ہر کسی کو احسان کی تلاش کی ترغیب دیتے ہوئے۔ رازی نے احسان کے تصور پر تفصیل سے بحث کی، یہ وضاحت کرتے ہوئے کہ اس میں اللہ تعالیٰ کے ساتھ، اپنے آپ کے ساتھ، اور دوسروں کے ساتھ اپنے تعلق کو کامل کرنا شامل ہے، اور ایسی بہترین کبھی بغیر انعام کے نہیں رہتی۔ طبری نے روایات ریکارڈ کیں کہ اللہ تعالیٰ محسنین سے محبت کرتا ہے اور انہیں خاص انعامات دیتا ہے۔ دونوں روایات اس آیت کو استعمال کرتی ہیں تاکہ مومنوں کو احسان کی تلاش کی ترغیب دیں۔
110.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تُؤسِّس مبدأ الله الثابت في مجازاة من يتميَّزون في الإيمان والعمل الصالح. ويُوضِّح ابن كثير أن الآية تُعمِّم من مثال إبراهيم الخاص إلى جميع المؤمنين محثَّةً على السعي للإحسان في كل جانب من جوانب الحياة. ويتناول الرازي مفهوم الإحسان تناولاً مستفيضاً مُبيِّناً أنه يستلزم إتقان العلاقة مع الله ومع النفس ومع الآخرين، وأن هذا الكمال لا يمرُّ بلا جزاء في نظام الله العادل. ويُلاحِظ الطبري أن الآية تَرِد في القرآن في صيغ مشابهة متكررة مُؤسِّسةً الجزاء على الصلاح مبدأ إلهياً جوهرياً شاملاً. ويُشدِّد القرطبي على أن الجزاء دنيوي وأخروي معاً: حسن السمعة والتأثير المبارك واليسر في الدنيا والجنة ورضوان الله في الآخرة. ويُشدِّد علماء الشيعة خصوصاً على أن الآية تدعو جميع المؤمنين إلى الاقتداء بإبراهيم إذ التميُّز الروحي ليس حكراً على الأنبياء بل في متناول كل من يسعى صادقاً مخلصاً. ويُوضِّح المفسر السني البيضاوي أن «كذلك» يُشير إلى أن طريقة الله في مكافأة إبراهيم تُحدِّد النمط الذي يكافئ به المحسنين جميعاً. ويتفق التراثان على أن الإحسان يمثِّل أرقى درجات الممارسة الإسلامية تتجاوز الطاعة المجردة لتبلغ الجمال والكمال في جميع وجوه الإيمان، والجميع يُعلِّمون أن هذه الآية بشارة وأمل تُؤكِّد أن السعي الصالح لا يضيع وأن عدل الله يكفل الجزاء المناسب لكل عمل حسن.
110.layer1: Verse 110 concludes this segment with a universal principle: 'Indeed, We thus reward the doers of good.' The Arabic 'kadhalika najzi al-muhsineen' — 'thus do We reward the muhsineen' — is a sweeping divine statement that extends the honor given to Ibrahim into a general law of how Allah deals with all people of excellence and goodness. The term 'muhsineen' comes from 'ihsan,' which the Prophet Muhammad explained as 'to worship Allah as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, know that He sees you.' Ihsan is therefore not merely doing good deeds but doing them with the highest level of awareness, sincerity, and excellence. The reward described for Ibrahim in the preceding verses — divine ransom, an enduring legacy, and Allah's own greeting of peace — is presented here not as a unique exception but as an example of how Allah always treats those who reach this level of devotion. This carries enormous encouragement for every believer: the same divine care, honor, and recognition that Ibrahim received is available to any servant of Allah who reaches the level of ihsan. The repetition of this phrase throughout Surah as-Saffat (appearing in reference to Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Harun, Ilyas, and Lut) creates a divine framework confirming that Allah's rewards for the righteous follow a consistent and reliable pattern. Believers are thus invited to emulate the muhsineen and trust that Allah's generosity toward them will be equally complete.
110.layer2: Al-Tabari in Jami al-Bayan explains that this verse establishes 'al-sunnat Allah fil-muhsineen' — the consistent way of Allah in dealing with those who excel in faith and obedience. He notes that the use of 'kadhalika' (thus, in this manner) at the opening of the verse points backward to everything that was done for Ibrahim — the ransom, the lasting legacy, the divine salutation — and declares all of it to be the pattern of divine reward for the doers of good. Ibn Kathir emphasizes that the verse creates a theological promise: excellence in worship and obedience to Allah will always be met with excellence in divine reward, and the story of Ibrahim is the supreme proof of this principle. Ibn Kathir also notes that the word 'muhsineen' connects to the famous hadith of Jibril recorded in Sahih Muslim, in which the Prophet defined ihsan as the highest level of religious practice — above Islam and iman — as it involves complete internal consciousness of Allah during every act. Al-Qurtubi draws attention to the significance of the first person plural 'najzi' (We reward) — Allah speaks as the direct and personal rewarder of the muhsineen, not through intermediaries or natural processes alone, but by His own direct divine action. Al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb explores the theological implication that this verse implies a divine covenant: ihsan toward Allah produces a guaranteed ihsan from Allah in return, establishing a relationship of reciprocal excellence between the Creator and His most devoted servants.
110.layer3: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran writes that this verse functions as the moral and theological heart of the entire Ibrahim narrative in Surah as-Saffat. The story is not merely a historical account of one prophet's trial but a declaration of how the entire divine system operates: sincere excellence in obedience to Allah always generates a corresponding excellence in divine reward. Qutb observes that the repetition of this formula throughout the surah — for prophet after prophet — builds a cumulative emotional and intellectual certainty in the listener's heart that this is indeed an unchanging divine law. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir connects the concept of 'ihsan' to its multidimensional meaning in Islamic ethics: excellence in worship, excellence in dealings with people, excellence in thought and intention, and excellence in facing trials. The muhsineen are not those who are merely technically correct in their religion but those who bring beauty, sincerity, and depth to everything they do for Allah's sake. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen in his explanations of Quranic passages emphasized that this verse should generate in the believer both aspiration and confidence — aspiration to reach the level of ihsan in one's own life, and confidence that Allah's promise of reward for the muhsineen is certain and comprehensive. Contemporary Islamic educators use this verse to encourage Muslims facing difficulty to understand that patient and sincere endurance of trials, combined with beautiful conduct toward Allah and creation, will inevitably produce divine recognition and reward in forms both seen and unseen, in this life and in the eternal life to come.

concepts.title: Our Servants
concepts.coreInsight: 'Our servants' ('ibadina) shows a relationship of belonging - Ibrahim isn't just any servant but one who belongs to Allah in a special, intimate way.
concepts.whyItMatters: Being Allah's servant isn't servitude but honor. It means belonging to the Most High, protected and valued by the Lord of all worlds.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'ہمارے بندے' ایک تعلق کی نشاندہی کرتا ہے - ابراہیم صرف کوئی بندہ نہیں بلکہ ایک خاص، قریبی طریقے سے اللہ سے تعلق رکھتے ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ کا بندہ ہونا غلامی نہیں بلکہ عزت ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'عبادنا' تُظهر علاقة انتماء - إبراهيم ليس مجرد عبد بل ينتمي لله بطريقة خاصة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: كون المرء عبداً لله ليس عبودية بل شرف.

concepts.title: Believing Servants
concepts.coreInsight: 'Al-mu'minin' (the believers) emphasizes that Ibrahim's defining quality was his unwavering faith - action and excellence flowed from his deep conviction.
concepts.whyItMatters: Right action begins with right belief. When faith is firm, excellence in deeds follows naturally. Strengthen your iman to strengthen your actions.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'مومنین' اس بات پر زور دیتا ہے کہ ابراہیم کی بنیادی خوبی ان کا غیر متزلزل ایمان تھا - عمل اور بہترینی ان کے گہرے یقین سے نکلی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: صحیح عمل صحیح عقیدے سے شروع ہوتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'المؤمنين' تؤكد أن الصفة المميزة لإبراهيم كانت إيمانه الثابت.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: العمل الصحيح يبدأ بالإيمان الصحيح.

concepts.title: Divine Affirmation
concepts.coreInsight: Allah confirms Ibrahim's status with 'Indeed, he was' - this is divine testimony, the highest form of character witness from the One who knows all hearts.
concepts.whyItMatters: Human praise is fleeting; Allah's affirmation is eternal. Seek to be among those whom Allah Himself testifies to as believers.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اللہ 'بے شک وہ تھے' کے ساتھ ابراہیم کی حیثیت کی تصدیق کرتا ہے - یہ الہی گواہی ہے، اس ذات کی سب سے اعلیٰ شکل جو تمام دلوں کو جانتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: انسانی تعریف عارضی ہے؛ اللہ کی تصدیق ابدی ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يؤكد الله مكانة إبراهيم بـ'إنه' - هذه شهادة إلهية، أعلى شكل من الشهادة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: المدح البشري زائل؛ تأكيد الله أبدي.

111.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse honors Ibrahim by describing him as one of Allah's believing servants, emphasizing that faith and servitude together constitute the highest human station. Ibn Kathir explains that the description as a believing servant confirms that Ibrahim's faith was genuine and complete, proven through his actions in the supreme trial. Al-Razi notes that the verse places Ibrahim within the community of righteous believers across history, showing that prophets and ordinary faithful servants form one spiritual family. Tabari emphasizes that being described as Allah's servant is itself a tremendous honor, indicating special closeness and favor. Qurtubi notes that the phrase 'Our servants' suggests ownership in the sense of special care and protection, as one protects what belongs to oneself. Shia scholars particularly emphasize that the greatest prophets, including Muhammad and Ibrahim, took pride in being servants of Allah rather than in worldly titles. Sunni commentator al-Baydawi explains that the combination of belief and servitude addresses both heart and action, the internal and external dimensions of religion. Both traditions agree that this verse establishes the criterion for true honor: not lineage, wealth, or power, but sincere faith expressed through humble obedience. All schools teach that the verse invites every believer to strive for this designation, making spiritual excellence accessible to all who sincerely submit to Allah.
111.layer4_urdu: سنی اور شیعہ دونوں علماء اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ آیت ابراہیم علیہ السلام کو اللہ تعالیٰ کے مومن بندوں میں سے ایک کے طور پر بیان کرکے ان کی عزت کرتی ہے، اس بات پر زور دیتے ہوئے کہ ایمان اور بندگی مل کر سب سے بلند انسانی مقام بناتے ہیں۔ ابن کثیر نے وضاحت کی کہ مومن بندے کے طور پر تفصیل تصدیق کرتی ہے کہ ابراہیم علیہ السلام کا ایمان حقیقی اور مکمل تھا، اعلیٰ امتحان میں ان کے اعمال کے ذریعے ثابت ہوا۔ رازی نے نوٹ کیا کہ آیت ابراہیم علیہ السلام کو تاریخ بھر میں نیک مومنوں کی برادری میں رکھتی ہے، یہ ظاہر کرتے ہوئے کہ انبیاء اور صالحین سب ایک ہی بنیادی خصوصیت شیئر کرتے ہیں: ایمان اور بندگی۔ طبری نے روایات ریکارڈ کیں کہ ابراہیم علیہ السلام کا ایمان اتنا مضبوط تھا کہ کوئی آزمائش اسے نہیں ہلا سکتی تھی۔
111.layer4_ar: يتفق العلماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تكرّم إبراهيم عليه السلام بوصفه من عباد الله المؤمنين، مؤكدةً أن الإيمان والعبودية معاً يمثلان أسمى مراتب الإنسانية عند الله. ويُبيِّن ابن كثير رحمه الله أن وصفه بالعبد المؤمن يثبت أن إيمانه كان كاملاً خالصاً، قد صدّقه العمل وأثبته الابتلاء. ويلاحظ الرازي أن الآية تضع إبراهيم ضمن مجتمع الصالحين عبر التاريخ مشيرةً إلى أن الأنبياء والمؤمنين يؤلفون أسرة روحية واحدة. ويؤكد الطبري أن وصفه بالعبد في حد ذاته مكانة رفيعة تدل على القرب الخاص والكرامة الإلهية. ويلاحظ القرطبي أن عبارة "عبادنا" تُوحي بالملكية بمعنى العناية والحماية الخاصة. ويؤكد علماء الشيعة خاصةً أن أعظم الأنبياء محمداً وإبراهيم عليهم الصلاة والسلام كانا يعتزان بعبوديتهما لله فوق كل لقب. ويُبيِّن المفسر السني البيضاوي أن الجمع بين الإيمان والعبودية يعالج البعدين الداخلي والخارجي، إيمان القلب وامتثال الجوارح. ويتفق التراثان على أن الآية تضع معيار الشرف الحقيقي لا في النسب أو الثروة أو السلطة بل في الإيمان الصادق المُعبَّر عنه بالطاعة المتواضعة. وتُعلِّم جميع المذاهب أن الآية تدعو كل مؤمن للسعي نحو هذا اللقب مُجعِلةً السمو الروحي متاحاً لكل من أخلص تسليمه لله.
111.layer1: Verse 111 concludes the magnificent narrative of Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son by affirming his standing with Allah: 'Indeed, he was of Our believing servants.' After Ibrahim passed the most severe of all trials, Allah honours him with this profound declaration of divine recognition. The word 'min ibadina al-muminin' (from Our believing servants) carries immense weight. It does not merely call Ibrahim a believer, but places him among a specially honoured group of sincere worshippers who have demonstrated their faith through action, not just words. This verse teaches Muslims that true iman (faith) is proved through steadfastness in trials, especially when what is most beloved to us is placed on the altar of obedience to Allah. Ibrahim's love for his son was immense, yet his love for Allah was greater. This is the defining quality of the sincere believer. Practically, this verse encourages Muslims facing hardship to see their trials as opportunities to demonstrate genuine faith. Scholars note that this verse, in the original Arabic, uses a possessive construction indicating closeness and divine approval, reminding us that when we surrender to Allah completely, we earn nearness to Him. The context of this Meccan surah, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad in Mecca when early Muslims faced severe persecution, provided them with Ibrahim's example as a source of immense comfort and inspiration to remain steadfast.
111.layer2: Imam Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan records that the declaration 'innahu min ibadina al-muminin' (he was of Our believing servants) serves as divine testimony to Ibrahim's complete faith and sincerity. Tabari cites the understanding of Ibn Abbas and Mujahid that this verse summarises the spiritual station Ibrahim achieved by submitting entirely to Allah's command regarding his son. Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim explains that this phrase is a divine attestation, functioning similarly to the phrase 'salam' (peace) that precedes it, as a mark of Allah's approval and honour. Ibn Kathir notes that the possessive form 'ibadina' (Our servants) denotes a special, intimate relationship with Allah, reserved for those who have proven their servitude beyond ordinary worship. The classical scholars understood this verse as a capstone to the sacrifice narrative, sealing Ibrahim's spiritual rank. Imam Qurtubi in his al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran draws attention to the use of the plural 'servants' indicating Ibrahim's membership in a distinguished community of prophets and the righteous, all characterised by verified, tested iman. The linguistic root of 'muminin' indicates active, ongoing faith, not a static condition, suggesting that Ibrahim's belief was alive and dynamic throughout the entire ordeal. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb further observes that the phrase identifies iman as the defining virtue that earned Ibrahim this closeness, making the verse a theological statement on the centrality of faith in Islamic soteriology.
111.layer3: Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, meditates deeply on this verse as the divine seal of approval on Ibrahim's journey of total surrender. He writes that Ibrahim's faith was not a theoretical conviction but a lived reality tested in the most extreme circumstances a father could face. Qutb emphasises that the Quran here uses 'ibadina al-muminin' to define a category of humans whose faith has been forged in the crucible of sacrifice. This resonates strongly in the modern context, where faith is often understood as a comfortable, intellectual assent rather than a transformative force that reshapes one's priorities and choices. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in al-Tafsir al-Munir highlights that this divine attestation to Ibrahim's faith should inspire every Muslim to aspire beyond routine worship to a state of genuine, tested iman. He links this verse to the broader Quranic theme of Allah knowing His servants deeply and honouring those who prove sincere. Ibn Uthaymeen, in his commentary traditions, often cited such verses to distinguish between genuine tawakkul (reliance on Allah) and passive inaction, noting that Ibrahim's faith was expressed through active obedience. Contemporary scholars also note that this verse, in the context of a Meccan surah, was a powerful message to the persecuted early Muslim community: those who hold firm to faith under pressure are among Allah's honoured servants. The verse continues to speak to Muslims today who navigate faith amid social, professional, or family pressures that test the sincerity of their belief.

concepts.title: Good Tidings
concepts.coreInsight: 'We gave him good tidings' (bashharnahu) - after the trial with one son, Allah promises another son, showing that trials are followed by blessings.
concepts.whyItMatters: Patience through difficulty leads to unexpected blessings. What we sacrifice for Allah is returned manifold in ways we couldn't imagine.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'ہم نے اسے خوشخبری دی' - ایک بیٹے کے ساتھ آزمائش کے بعد، اللہ دوسرے بیٹے کا وعدہ کرتا ہے، یہ دکھاتے ہوئے کہ آزمائشوں کے بعد برکتیں آتی ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: مشکلات میں صبر غیر متوقع برکتوں کی طرف لے جاتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'بشرناه' - بعد الابتلاء بابن، يعد الله بابن آخر، مما يُظهر أن المحن تتبعها البركات.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: الصبر في الصعوبات يؤدي إلى بركات غير متوقعة.

concepts.title: Isaac: A Prophet
concepts.coreInsight: Isaac (Ishaq) is specifically promised as 'a prophet' - his prophethood is announced before his birth, showing Allah's predetermined plan for righteous lineages.
concepts.whyItMatters: Allah prepares future generations of righteousness. Our faithfulness today shapes the spiritual legacy of our descendants.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اسحاق کو خاص طور پر 'ایک نبی' کے طور پر وعدہ دیا گیا ہے - ان کی نبوت ان کی پیدائش سے پہلے اعلان کی گئی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ صالح نسلوں کی آئندہ نسلیں تیار کرتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يُعد بإسحاق خصيصاً 'نبياً' - أُعلنت نبوته قبل ولادته.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: الله يُعد أجيالاً مستقبلية من الصالحين.

concepts.title: Among Righteous
concepts.coreInsight: 'From among the righteous' (min as-salihin) - Isaac's membership in the community of the righteous is declared even before his birth.
concepts.whyItMatters: Allah knows and decrees righteousness. When we strive for Allah's pleasure, He may write righteousness for our lineage as well.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'صالحوں میں سے' - اسحاق کی صالحوں کی جماعت میں شمولیت ان کی پیدائش سے پہلے ہی اعلان کر دی گئی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ صالحیت کو جانتا اور مقرر کرتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'من الصالحين' - يُعلن انضمام إسحاق لجماعة الصالحين حتى قبل ولادته.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: الله يعلم ويقدر الصلاح.

concepts.title: Prophetic Continuity
concepts.coreInsight: From Ibrahim comes Isaac, and from Isaac will come Ya'qub (Jacob) and then the Children of Israel - showing how one prophet's sacrifice echoes through generations.
concepts.whyItMatters: Our sacrifices create pathways for future blessings. One person's submission to Allah can illuminate the path for countless descendants.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: ابراہیم سے اسحاق آتے ہیں، اور اسحاق سے یعقوب اور پھر بنی اسرائیل آئیں گے - یہ دکھاتے ہوئے کہ ایک نبی کی قربانی نسلوں تک گونجتی ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ہماری قربانیاں مستقبل کی برکتوں کے راستے بناتی ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: من إبراهيم يأتي إسحاق، ومن إسحاق سيأتي يعقوب ثم بني إسرائيل.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: تضحياتنا تخلق مسارات للبركات المستقبلية.

112.layer4: Shia and Sunni scholars differ significantly on the implications of this verse for identifying which son Ibrahim was commanded to sacrifice. Shia scholars, following hadith from the Ahlul Bayt, cite this verse as decisive proof that Ismail was the intended sacrifice, since Isaac's birth is announced after the sacrifice narrative. Ibn Abbas and other early Muslim scholars also held this position. However, some Sunni commentators argue that the Quranic narrative is not necessarily chronological. Ibn Kathir presents both views but acknowledges that the placement of Isaac's birth announcement after the sacrifice story suggests Ismail was the intended sacrifice. Al-Razi discusses the chronological argument in detail, noting that the sequence of Quranic verses typically follows chronological order unless there is clear indication otherwise. Tabari records numerous early Islamic authorities who identified Ismail as the sacrifice based on this verse's placement. Qurtubi acknowledges the strength of the argument based on verse sequence but also presents alternative views. Despite this difference, both traditions agree that Isaac became a great prophet from among the righteous, fulfilling Allah's promise to Ibrahim. Both schools emphasize that Allah blessed Ibrahim abundantly with multiple prophetic sons, demonstrating divine reward for faithfulness. All scholars agree that the birth announcement was miraculous, occurring when both parents were beyond normal childbearing age, demonstrating Allah's power over natural law.
112.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی علماء اس آیت کے مضمرات پر نمایاں طور پر مختلف ہیں کہ کس بیٹے کو ابراہیم علیہ السلام نے قربان کرنے کا حکم دیا گیا تھا۔ شیعہ علماء، اہل بیت علیہم السلام سے حدیث کی پیروی کرتے ہوئے، اس آیت کو فیصلہ کن ثبوت کے طور پر پیش کرتے ہیں کہ اسماعیل علیہ السلام مقصودہ قربانی تھے، کیونکہ اسحاق علیہ السلام کی پیدائش قربانی کی روایت کے بعد اعلان کی گئی ہے۔ ابن عباس رضی اللہ عنہ اور دیگر ابتدائی مسلم علماء نے بھی یہ موقف اختیار کیا۔ تاہم، کچھ سنی مفسرین دلیل دیتے ہیں کہ قرآنی روایت لازمی طور پر تاریخی ترتیب میں نہیں ہے۔ ابن کثیر دونوں خیالات پیش کرتے ہیں لیکن نوٹ کرتے ہیں کہ ابتدائی علماء کی اکثریت نے اسماعیل علیہ السلام کو قربانی کے طور پر شناخت کیا۔ دونوں روایات اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ اسحاق علیہ السلام ایک مبارک نبی تھے جن کی نسل سے بہت سے انبیاء آئے۔
112.layer4_ar: يختلف العلماء الشيعة والسنة اختلافاً واضحاً في ما تترتب عليه هذه الآية من تحديد الابن الذي أُمر إبراهيم بذبحه. فيستشهد العلماء الشيعة بالروايات الواردة عن أهل البيت عليهم السلام ويستدلون بهذه الآية دليلاً حاسماً على أن إسماعيل هو الذبيح، لمجيء البشارة بولادة إسحاق بعد قصة الذبح لا قبلها. وقد كان ابن عباس وعدد من علماء السلف على هذا القول أيضاً. غير أن بعض المفسرين السنيين يرون أن السياق القرآني لا يسير بالضرورة وفق الترتيب الزمني. ويعرض ابن كثير الرأيين كليهما لكنه يُقر بأن مجيء البشارة بولادة إسحاق بعد قصة الذبح يرجّح أن إسماعيل هو الذبيح. ويتناول الرازي الحجة الزمنية بالتفصيل، مُنبِّهاً إلى أن آيات القرآن تسير وفق الترتيب الزمني ما لم تدل قرينة صريحة على خلاف ذلك. ويُسجِّل الطبري جملةً من علماء الإسلام الأوائل الذين رأوا أن إسماعيل هو الذبيح استناداً إلى موضع هذه الآية. ويُقر القرطبي بقوة الحجة المبنية على ترتيب الآيات وإن نقل آراء أخرى. وعلى الرغم من هذا الخلاف، يتفق التراثان على أن إسحاق كان نبياً عظيماً من الصالحين وأن وعد الله لإبراهيم تحقق، وأن ولادته كانت معجزة تجلّت فيها قدرة الله على تجاوز قوانين الطبيعة.
112.layer1: Verse 112 announces the second great blessing upon Ibrahim: 'And We gave him glad tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.' After the trial of the sacrifice, Allah rewarded Ibrahim with the good news that his second son, Isaac (Ishaq), would also be a prophet and among the righteous. This reward demonstrates a profound divine principle: when a believer sacrifices something beloved for Allah's sake, Allah compensates with something even greater. The mention of Isaac immediately after the sacrifice narrative is significant. Many classical scholars held that the son brought for sacrifice was Ismail, and that the announcement of Isaac came as an additional blessing, meaning Ibrahim would have two prophetic sons. The term 'nabi' (prophet) indicates a formal divine appointment, while 'min al-salihin' (from the righteous) confirms not merely his official role but his personal virtue and character. This verse also reminds us that Allah's blessings often come in waves, one after another. Ibrahim was given the trial of the sacrifice, passed it with complete surrender, was honoured as a believing servant, and then immediately granted the news of another righteous prophet from his lineage. Practically, this teaches Muslims that obedience to Allah opens doors of blessing that disobedience and attachment to worldly things would close. The glad tidings of Isaac also foreshadow the chain of prophethood that would flow through his descendants, including the great line of Israelite prophets.
112.layer2: The announcement in verse 112 of Isaac's prophethood prompted significant scholarly discussion in classical tafsir. Imam Tabari provides extensive narrations in his Jami al-Bayan regarding whether the sacrificed son was Ismail or Isaac. Tabari himself acknowledged that both opinions had scholarly support among the Companions and the Tabi'un (second generation). He noted that Ibn Abbas at times said the sacrificed son was Ismail, as did Jabir ibn Abd Allah and Abu Hurayra. The significance of the placement of this glad tidings immediately after the sacrifice narrative is highlighted by Ibn Kathir, who argues in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim that if Isaac were the sacrificed son, it would be strange for his good news to be announced as a new blessing in the same breath, since he had already been mentioned. Ibn Kathir concludes this strengthens the view that Ismail was the son of sacrifice, and Isaac's prophethood was an additional divine gift. Imam Qurtubi examines the dual nature of the glad tidings: the announcement carries both the news of a new child and the confirmation of his prophetic status, making it doubly joyful. Al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb notes the beautiful structure of the verse wherein 'nabiyyan' (a prophet) and 'min al-salihin' (from the righteous) together define Isaac's identity in terms of both his divine mission and his moral character. This suggests that prophethood and personal righteousness are inseparable in Quranic discourse about the prophets.
112.layer3: Modern Sunni scholars reflect on verse 112 to draw out its theological and inspirational dimensions. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in al-Tafsir al-Munir notes that the glad tidings given to Ibrahim serve as a model of how divine generosity flows from acts of sincere sacrifice. Al-Zuhayli connects this to the concept of istidraj in reverse, where the righteous are not tested to be destroyed but to be elevated, and their reward is multiplied beyond the sacrifice they made. Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, reflects on the spiritual economy of the Quran in which no sincere act of surrender goes unrewarded. He notes that Ibrahim offered his son, and Allah gave him back his son and then granted him another, Isaac, who would carry the light of prophethood. For Qutb, this reflects the Quranic logic that the believer who gives everything to Allah loses nothing and gains everything. Contemporary scholars, including those influenced by the pedagogical approach of Muhammad al-Sha'rawi, observe that the word 'bashsharnahum' (We gave glad tidings) is an act of divine speech directly addressed to Ibrahim, indicating the intimacy of the relationship between Allah and his closest servants. The mention of Isaac as both prophet and righteous is a reminder that the qualities we most deeply hope to instil in our children, piety and righteousness, are themselves gifts from Allah, not merely the product of parenting or education alone.

concepts.title: Divine Blessing
concepts.coreInsight: 'We blessed him and Isaac' (barakna 'alayhi wa 'ala Ishaq) - Allah's blessing encompasses both father and son, multiplying their impact and legacy.
concepts.whyItMatters: Allah's blessing doesn't just touch individuals but extends to their relationships and offspring, creating blessed lineages.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'ہم نے اسے اور اسحاق کو برکت دی' - اللہ کی برکت باپ اور بیٹے دونوں کو شامل کرتی ہے، ان کے اثر اور میراث کو بڑھاتی ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ کی برکت صرف افراد کو نہیں چھوتی بلکہ ان کے تعلقات اور اولاد تک پھیل جاتی ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'باركنا عليه وعلى إسحاق' - بركة الله تشمل الأب والابن، تضاعف أثرهما وإرثهما.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: بركة الله لا تلمس الأفراد فقط بل تمتد لعلاقاتهم وذريتهم.

concepts.title: Dual Destiny
concepts.coreInsight: 'Among their descendants is the doer of good and the clearly unjust to himself' - from blessed lineages come both righteousness and rebellion. Piety isn't inherited automatically.
concepts.whyItMatters: Being descended from righteous ancestors guarantees nothing. Each person must choose their own path - bloodline doesn't equal righteousness.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'ان کی اولاد میں نیکوکار اور اپنے اوپر ظلم کرنے والے دونوں ہیں' - مبارک نسلوں سے نیکی اور بغاوت دونوں آتے ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: نیک آباؤ اجداد سے تعلق کچھ ضمانت نہیں دیتا۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'من ذريتهما محسن وظالم لنفسه' - من النسل المبارك يأتي الصلاح والطغيان.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: الانحدار من أجداد صالحين لا يضمن شيئاً.

concepts.title: Self-Injustice
concepts.coreInsight: 'Unjust to himself' (zalimun linafsihi) - sin is described as self-harm. The sinner doesn't hurt Allah but wounds their own soul.
concepts.whyItMatters: Every sin is an act of self-sabotage. When we disobey Allah, we harm ourselves, not Him. Understanding this reframes repentance as self-care.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'اپنے آپ پر ظالم' - گناہ کو خود کو نقصان پہنچانے کے طور پر بیان کیا گیا ہے۔ گناہگار اللہ کو تکلیف نہیں دیتا بلکہ اپنی روح کو زخمی کرتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ہر گناہ خود کو نقصان پہنچانے کا عمل ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'ظالم لنفسه' - الخطيئة موصوفة كأذى للنفس. المذنب لا يؤذي الله بل يجرح روحه.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: كل خطيئة هي فعل إيذاء للنفس.

concepts.title: Free Will
concepts.coreInsight: This verse is a divine reminder of human free will - even from the most blessed lineages, individuals still choose their own spiritual destiny.
concepts.whyItMatters: Your choices define you, not your ancestry. Use your free will to join the muhsinin (doers of good), regardless of your background.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: یہ آیت انسانی آزاد مرضی کی الہی یاد دہانی ہے - سب سے زیادہ مبارک نسلوں سے بھی، افراد اپنی روحانی تقدیر کا انتخاب کرتے ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: آپ کے انتخاب آپ کی تعریف کرتے ہیں، نہ کہ آپ کے آباؤ اجداد۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: هذه الآية تذكير إلهي بإرادة الإنسان الحرة - حتى من أكثر الأنساب بركة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: اختياراتك تحددك، ليس نسبك.

113.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse teaches that righteousness is not inherited and that among the descendants of Ibrahim and Isaac were both righteous people and sinners. Ibn Kathir explains that the verse refers particularly to the children of Israel, among whom were many prophets and righteous people but also many who disobeyed and rejected prophetic guidance. Al-Razi emphasizes that divine blessing upon ancestors does not automatically transfer to descendants; each generation and individual must earn righteousness through their own faith and actions. Tabari notes that the phrase 'clearly unjust to himself' indicates that such people harm themselves obviously and undeniably through their sins. Qurtubi explains that the division between righteous and unjust exists in every community, even those with the most blessed ancestry, demonstrating that lineage does not determine spiritual status. Shia scholars particularly emphasize the verse as warning against pride in ancestry, teaching that what matters is personal taqwa and righteous action. Sunni commentator al-Baydawi notes that being unjust to oneself means harming one's own soul through sin and disbelief, the ultimate form of self-destruction. Both traditions agree that the verse establishes individual accountability in faith; no one can rely on the righteousness of their family or community without personal commitment. All schools teach that the verse provides balanced perspective: acknowledging that blessed lineages produce many righteous people while warning that blessing and guidance do not override free will.
113.layer4_urdu: سنی اور شیعہ دونوں علماء اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ آیت سکھاتی ہے کہ نیکی میراثی نہیں ہے اور ابراہیم علیہ السلام اور اسحاق علیہ السلام کی نسلوں میں نیک لوگ اور گنہگار دونوں تھے۔ ابن کثیر نے وضاحت کی کہ آیت خاص طور پر بنی اسرائیل کی طرف اشارہ کرتی ہے، جن میں بہت سے نبی اور نیک لوگ تھے لیکن بہت سے ایسے بھی تھے جنہوں نے نافرمانی کی اور نبوی رہنمائی کو مسترد کیا۔ رازی نے زور دیا کہ آباؤ اجداد پر الہی برکت خودکار طور پر نسلوں کو منتقل نہیں ہوتی؛ ہر نسل کو اپنے لیے ایمان منتخب کرنا چاہیے۔ طبری نے روایات ریکارڈ کیں کہ کس طرح بنی اسرائیل میں انبیاء اور گنہگار دونوں تھے۔ دونوں روایات اس آیت کو استعمال کرتی ہیں تاکہ میراثی شرافت کے جھوٹے دعووں کو مسترد کریں اور انفرادی ذمہ داری پر زور دیں۔
113.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن الآية تُعلِّم أن الصلاح لا يُورَث وأن في ذرية إبراهيم وإسحاق صالحين وطالحين. ويُبيِّن ابن كثير أن الآية تُشير بصفة خاصة إلى بني إسرائيل الذين كان فيهم أنبياء كثيرون وصالحون وكان فيهم أيضاً من عصى الأنبياء ورفض الهداية. ويُؤكِّد الرازي أن بركة الآباء لا تنتقل أوتوماتيكياً إلى الأبناء، وأن كل جيل وكل فرد مطالب بكسب صلاحه بإيمانه الخاص وعمله الشخصي. ويُنبِّه الطبري إلى أن عبارة "الظالم لنفسه مبيناً" تدل على أن هؤلاء يؤذون أنفسهم بصورة جلية لا تقبل الإنكار. ويُبيِّن القرطبي أن الانقسام بين الصالح والطالح قائم في كل أمة حتى الأكثر بركةً في نسبها، مؤكداً أن النسب لا يُقرِّر المآل الروحي. ويُؤكِّد العلماء الشيعة خاصةً أن الآية تُحذِّر من الغرور بالانتساب، ومحور الاعتبار هو التقوى الشخصية والعمل الصالح. ويُوضِّح المفسر السني البيضاوي أن ظلم النفس يعني الإضرار بالروح بالذنب والكفر وهو أشد صور الإضرار بالنفس. ويتفق التراثان على أن الآية تُرسي المساءلة الفردية في الإيمان ولا يجوز لأحد أن يتكل على صلاح أسرته أو مجتمعه من غير التزام شخصي.
113.layer1: Verse 113 states: 'And We blessed him and Isaac; and among their progeny are those who do good, and those who plainly wrong themselves.' This verse conveys two powerful messages simultaneously. First, it affirms the divine blessing upon Ibrahim and his son Isaac, a comprehensive blessing encompassing prophethood, righteous descendants, and lasting honour. Second, it acknowledges with remarkable honesty that not all descendants of prophets follow the path of righteousness. The phrase 'wa min dhurriyyatihima muhsin wa zalim li-nafsihi mubin' (and among their progeny are those who do good and those who plainly wrong themselves) is a frank and honest statement about human freedom. Even the children and grandchildren of prophets are not guaranteed righteousness; each soul makes its own choices. This serves to dispel the notion that birth into a prophetic lineage guarantees salvation or righteousness. The Quran consistently affirms individual moral responsibility across all family lines. The word 'zalim li-nafsihi mubin' (those who plainly wrong themselves) uses the word 'mubin' meaning clear or evident, indicating that the wrongdoing of the misguided among Ibrahim's progeny was not hidden but openly manifest. Practically, this verse teaches Muslims that while we should seek righteous company and lineage, our own choices and deeds are what ultimately define us before Allah. No family name, no tribal honour, and no prophetic ancestry can substitute for personal obedience and faith.
113.layer2: Classical scholars paid great attention to the comprehensive yet sobering content of verse 113. Imam Tabari, in Jami al-Bayan, explains that the blessing mentioned in the phrase 'barakna alayhi wa ala Ishaq' encompasses all forms of divine favour including prophethood, numerous righteous descendants, and the perpetuation of revelation through their lineage. He records that the scholars of tafsir among the Salaf understood the mention of 'muhsin' (righteous) and 'zalim li-nafsih' (wrongdoer of his own soul) as an acknowledgment that even prophetic families contain both types of individuals, thus underscoring the Quranic insistence on individual responsibility. Ibn Kathir emphasises in his Tafsir that 'barakna' refers to a lasting, expansive blessing that was not limited to the lifetime of Ibrahim and Isaac but extended through their generations to include all the prophets of Bani Israel and eventually the Prophet Muhammad through the Ishmaelite lineage. Imam Qurtubi uses this verse in al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran to address a theological point: that divine blessing upon a lineage does not imply predestination of all individuals in that lineage to righteousness. Free will and human choice remain operative even within divinely blessed families. Al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb provides a philosophical reflection, noting that the co-existence of righteous and wrongdoing descendants within the same divinely blessed family demonstrates the perfection of Allah's divine plan, which operates through human freedom rather than compulsion.
113.layer3: Sayyid Qutb, in Fi Zilal al-Quran, describes verse 113 as containing one of the Quran's most honest and realistic statements about human nature and prophetic legacy. He notes that the Quran does not idealise or romanticise the descendants of the prophets but presents the full truth: that divine blessing creates the environment and potential for righteousness, but each human being must choose. This realism is, for Qutb, itself evidence of the Quran's divine origin, as no human author seeking to glorify a prophetic lineage would include such a candid admission. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in al-Tafsir al-Munir contextualises the verse within Islamic teachings on genealogy and piety, citing the famous hadith of the Prophet who warned his own family that their kinship to him would not avail them if they failed to do righteous deeds. Al-Zuhayli emphasises that the blessing of Allah, 'barakah', is not a static inheritance but a living reality that each generation must strive to deserve and maintain through obedience and worship. In a contemporary context, this verse speaks powerfully to communities and families that may rely on ancestral piety or religious lineage as a substitute for personal practice and accountability. Ibn Uthaymeen's broader teachings consistently returned to this Quranic principle: that Allah judges individuals on their own deeds, and that the honour of righteous ancestors is a source of inspiration, not a guarantee of divine favour for those who do not themselves walk the path of righteousness.

concepts.title: Divine Favor
concepts.coreInsight: 'We conferred favor' (mananna) upon Musa and Harun - Allah granted them grace and blessings before they earned them, preparing them for their prophetic mission.
concepts.whyItMatters: Allah's favor precedes our worthiness. He equips us before He sends us. Trust that if He calls you to something, He has already prepared you for it.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'ہم نے احسان کیا' موسیٰ اور ہارون پر - اللہ نے انہیں فضل اور برکتیں دیں اس سے پہلے کہ وہ ان کے مستحق ہوں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ کا فضل ہماری اہلیت سے پہلے آتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'مننا' على موسى وهارون - منحهم الله نعمة وبركات قبل أن يستحقوها.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: فضل الله يسبق استحقاقنا.

concepts.title: Brotherly Partnership
concepts.coreInsight: Musa and Harun are mentioned together - they shared the prophetic mission as brothers, showing that sometimes Allah assigns tasks to teams, not just individuals.
concepts.whyItMatters: We don't have to carry our missions alone. Allah may provide companions to share the burden and strengthen us in righteousness.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: موسیٰ اور ہارون کا ایک ساتھ ذکر ہے - انہوں نے بھائیوں کے طور پر نبوی مشن کو شیئر کیا، یہ دکھاتے ہوئے کہ کبھی اللہ ٹیموں کو کام سونپتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ہمیں اپنے مشن اکیلے اٹھانے کی ضرورت نہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يُذكر موسى وهارون معاً - تقاسما الرسالة النبوية كأخوين.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: لا يجب أن نحمل مهامنا وحدنا.

concepts.title: New Chapter
concepts.coreInsight: The narrative shifts from Ibrahim's story to Musa's - connecting different prophets shows the continuity of divine guidance across time and peoples.
concepts.whyItMatters: The same God who guided Ibrahim guided Musa. His message is consistent, His mercy unchanging, His support available to all who call on Him.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: بیانیہ ابراہیم کی کہانی سے موسیٰ کی طرف منتقل ہوتا ہے - مختلف نبیوں کو جوڑنا وقت اور قوموں کے پار الہی رہنمائی کی تسلسل کو دکھاتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: وہی خدا جس نے ابراہیم کی رہنمائی کی، موسیٰ کی رہنمائی کی۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: ينتقل السرد من قصة إبراهيم إلى موسى - ربط الأنبياء المختلفين يُظهر استمرارية الهداية الإلهية.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: نفس الإله الذي هدى إبراهيم هدى موسى.

114.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse introduces the narrative of Moses and Aaron by emphasizing the divine favor bestowed upon them. Ibn Kathir explains that the favor included their selection for prophethood, their preservation from Pharaoh's persecution, the miracles they were granted, and their ultimate success in delivering the Israelites. Al-Razi notes that mentioning both prophets together highlights the importance of mutual support in fulfilling divine missions; Aaron's role as Moses's supportive partner was itself part of Allah's favor. Tabari emphasizes that the favor was comprehensive, including spiritual blessings like revelation and practical blessings like protection and success. Qurtubi notes that the emphatic phrasing 'We did certainly confer favor' indicates that this blessing is beyond dispute and serves as foundation for all that follows in their story. Shia scholars particularly emphasize the connection between this narrative and Ibrahim's story; both demonstrate divine patterns of selecting righteous servants, testing them, and granting them ultimate success. Sunni commentator al-Baydawi explains that divine favor in the Quran typically includes both blessing and responsibility, privilege and obligation. Both traditions agree that the story of Moses and Aaron provides crucial lessons about confronting tyranny, trusting in divine support, and persevering in mission despite obstacles. All schools teach that the verse encourages believers to recognize and be grateful for divine favors while dedicating themselves to fulfilling the responsibilities that accompany such blessings.
114.layer4_urdu: سنی اور شیعہ دونوں علماء اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ آیت موسیٰ علیہ السلام اور ہارون علیہ السلام کی روایت کو ان پر عطا کردہ الہی احسان پر زور دیتے ہوئے متعارف کراتی ہے۔ ابن کثیر نے وضاحت کی کہ احسان میں نبوت کے لیے ان کا انتخاب، فرعون کے ظلم سے ان کی حفاظت، جو معجزات انہیں دیے گئے، اور بنی اسرائیل کو پہنچانے میں ان کی حتمی کامیابی شامل تھی۔ رازی نے نوٹ کیا کہ دونوں نبیوں کا ایک ساتھ ذکر کرنا الہی مشنوں کو پورا کرنے میں باہمی مدد کی اہمیت کو اجاگر کرتا ہے؛ موسیٰ علیہ السلام کی کامیابی میں ہارون علیہ السلام کا کردار ضروری تھا۔ طبری نے روایات ریکارڈ کیں کہ کس طرح موسیٰ علیہ السلام اور ہارون علیہ السلام نے فرعون کے ظلم کا مقابلہ کرنے میں مل کر کام کیا۔
114.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن الآية تُقدِّم قصة موسى وهارون بالتنويه إلى النعمة الإلهية التي اختصّهما بها. ويُبيِّن ابن كثير أن النعمة شملت اصطفاءهما للنبوة ونجاتهما من بطش فرعون والمعجزات التي أُعطيا وانتصارهما في تحرير بني إسرائيل. ويُلاحِظ الرازي أن ذكر النبيين معاً يُبرز أهمية المساندة المتبادلة في الرسالات الإلهية وكون دور هارون المساند جزءاً من نعمة الله ذاتها. ويؤكد الطبري أن النعمة كانت شاملة للبركات الروحية والمادية. ويُلاحِظ القرطبي أن صيغة التأكيد "ولقد مننّا" تدل على أن هذه النعمة لا خلاف فيها وتُشكِّل الأساس الذي يقوم عليه كل ما يأتي في القصة. ويُؤكِّد العلماء الشيعة خاصةً الصلة بين هذه القصة وقصة إبراهيم من حيث تجليهما نمطاً إلهياً موحداً في انتقاء العباد الصالحين وابتلائهم ومنحهم الفتح. ويُوضِّح المفسر السني البيضاوي أن النعمة الإلهية في القرآن تجمع عادةً بين البركة والمسؤولية والامتياز والالتزام. ويتفق التراثان على أن قصة موسى وهارون تحمل دروساً بالغة الأهمية في مواجهة الطغيان والتوكل على العون الإلهي والصمود في الرسالة أمام العقبات والمحن.
114.layer1: Verse 114 opens a new prophetic narrative: 'And indeed We bestowed Our favour upon Moses and Aaron.' After the extended account of Ibrahim and the sacrifice, the Quran briefly but powerfully invokes the story of two other great prophets, Moses and Aaron, as a further example of divine grace to those who were chosen as messengers. The phrase 'wa laqad mananna ala Musa wa Harun' uses 'laqad' as an oath particle, emphasising certainty, and 'mananna' from the root meaning to bestow favour or grace, indicating the generous and complete nature of what Allah granted them. Moses and Aaron together form one of the most remarkable partnerships in prophetic history: Moses received revelation and leadership, while Aaron was given to him as a helper and companion in the monumental task of confronting Pharaoh and liberating the Children of Israel from centuries of oppression. This verse reminds Muslims that divine favour often comes in the form of support systems. Allah gave Moses his brother. The favour of companionship, of having someone alongside us in our mission, is itself a form of divine grace. This has practical implications for how Muslims should value their communities, families, and support networks as gifts from Allah. The mention of both prophets together also signals that collective blessing and mission are honoured in the Quran just as individual righteousness is honoured.
114.layer2: Imam Tabari in Jami al-Bayan records that the divine favour bestowed upon Moses and Aaron in verse 114 included prophethood, divine revelation, the Torah, miracles, and ultimately deliverance from Pharaoh's tyranny. Tabari cites early Islamic authorities who understood 'mananna' (We bestowed favour) as encompassing both spiritual and material blessings, including divine guidance, the covenant of prophethood, and the practical victory over the oppressive Egyptian regime. Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim notes that the pairing of Moses and Aaron in a single verse of divine favour reflects their joint mission, as confirmed in Surah Taha where Allah grants Moses his brother Aaron as a minister and assistant. Ibn Kathir highlights the significance of the Quran mentioning Aaron alongside Moses as co-recipients of divine favour, showing that supportive roles in the work of prophethood are also divinely honoured. Imam Qurtubi in al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran emphasises that the term 'manna' (favour or grace) in this verse is one of the highest expressions of divine generosity in the Quran, used specifically for the greatest of prophets. Al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb observes that the narrative shift from Ibrahim to Moses and Aaron follows a structural pattern in As-Saffat, where multiple prophetic stories are recounted to establish the consistency of divine support for all those who strive faithfully in Allah's path, and to demonstrate to the Prophet Muhammad that he stands in a long, honoured line of divinely supported messengers.
114.layer3: Contemporary scholars find rich meaning in the pairing of Moses and Aaron in verse 114. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reflects on how the divine favour to both prophets illustrates that the work of calling people to truth is not always a solitary endeavour. Moses, who felt his own eloquence was limited, was given Aaron as a companion and speaker, and together their complementary strengths formed a more complete and powerful prophetic mission. Qutb draws the lesson that movements for truth and justice in every age require collaboration, mutual support, and the recognition that individual strengths serve larger collective purposes. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in al-Tafsir al-Munir notes that the structural placement of this verse, immediately following the Ibrahim and Isaac narrative, reflects the Quran's method of presenting the prophetic tradition as a continuous chain of divine grace. Al-Zuhayli emphasises that every generation of faithful servants receives the favour appropriate to their mission and their time. Muhammad al-Sha'rawi's pedagogical tradition encourages reflection on how the same word 'mananna' used for Moses and Aaron connects to the Quranic idea that Allah's blessings take many forms: sometimes prophethood, sometimes a righteous companion, sometimes guidance at a critical moment. In the modern context, this verse inspires Islamic organisations and communities to see collaborative leadership not as a dilution of mission but as a form of divine wisdom, mirroring the model of Moses and Aaron.

concepts.title: Collective Salvation
concepts.coreInsight: 'We saved them and their people' - Allah's mercy extended beyond just the prophets to include Bani Israel, showing that righteous leaders bring salvation to their communities.
concepts.whyItMatters: Your righteousness can become a means of blessing for those around you. When Allah favors you, He may extend that favor to your community.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'ہم نے انہیں اور ان کی قوم کو بچایا' - اللہ کی رحمت صرف انبیاء سے آگے بنی اسرائیل تک پھیلی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: آپ کی صالحیت آپ کے ارد گرد والوں کے لیے برکت کا ذریعہ بن سکتی ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'نجيناهما وقومهما' - امتدت رحمة الله إلى ما وراء الأنبياء لتشمل بني إسرائيل.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: صلاحك يمكن أن يصبح وسيلة بركة لمن حولك.

concepts.title: Great Affliction
concepts.coreInsight: 'The great affliction' (al-karb al-azim) refers to Pharaoh's oppression - the enslavement, killing of infant boys, and systematic dehumanization of a people.
concepts.whyItMatters: Allah sees and responds to systemic injustice. No oppression, no matter how powerful, is beyond His ability to dismantle.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'عظیم مصیبت' فرعون کے ظلم کی طرف اشارہ کرتی ہے - غلامی، بچوں کی ہلاکت، اور ایک قوم کی منظم طریقے سے انسانیت سوزی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ نظامی ظلم کو دیکھتا اور جواب دیتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'الكرب العظيم' يشير إلى اضطهاد فرعون - الاستعباد وقتل الأطفال.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: الله يرى ويستجيب للظلم المنهجي.

concepts.title: Divine Deliverance
concepts.coreInsight: 'We saved' (najjayna) uses the intensive form - Allah's deliverance was complete and miraculous, parting the sea and destroying Pharaoh's army.
concepts.whyItMatters: When Allah delivers, He does so completely. No matter how impossible your situation seems, His power to save is unlimited.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'ہم نے بچایا' شدید صیغہ استعمال کرتا ہے - اللہ کی نجات مکمل اور معجزاتی تھی، سمندر کو چیرنا اور فرعون کی فوج کو تباہ کرنا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: جب اللہ نجات دیتا ہے، تو مکمل طور پر۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'نجيناهما' يستخدم الصيغة المشددة - كان إنقاذ الله كاملاً ومعجزياً.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: عندما ينقذ الله، يفعل ذلك بالكامل.

115.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse refers to Allah's deliverance of Moses, Aaron, and the Israelites from Pharaoh's oppression through the miraculous parting of the Red Sea. Ibn Kathir provides extensive detail about the affliction, describing Pharaoh's enslavement of the Israelites, forced labor, systematic infanticide, and brutal persecution. Al-Razi emphasizes that the salvation was comprehensive, including physical deliverance from slavery, spiritual liberation from oppressive environment, and psychological vindication through the destruction of their oppressors. Tabari records numerous traditions describing the dramatic escape through the parted sea and the drowning of Pharaoh's pursuing army. Qurtubi notes that calling it 'great affliction' indicates its severity and comprehensiveness, affecting every aspect of the Israelites' lives. Shia scholars particularly emphasize the verse as demonstrating divine justice and the inevitable triumph of truth over tyranny, providing hope to oppressed communities throughout history. Sunni commentator al-Baydawi explains that the salvation came after long patient endurance, teaching that divine deliverance requires perseverance and trust. Both traditions agree that the story provides crucial lessons about confronting oppression, trusting in divine assistance, and recognizing that Allah has power to deliver even when circumstances appear hopeless. All schools teach that the verse encourages gratitude for divine deliverance and confidence that Allah's support for the oppressed against oppressors is a consistent divine principle.
115.layer4_urdu: سنی اور شیعہ دونوں علماء اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ آیت بحیرہ احمر کے معجزانہ الگ ہونے کے ذریعے موسیٰ علیہ السلام، ہارون علیہ السلام، اور بنی اسرائیل کی فرعون کے ظلم سے اللہ تعالیٰ کی نجات کی طرف اشارہ کرتی ہے۔ ابن کثیر نے مصیبت کے بارے میں تفصیلی تفصیل فراہم کی، فرعون کی بنی اسرائیل کی غلامی، جبری مزدوری، منظم بچہ کشی، اور وحشیانہ ظلم کو بیان کرتے ہوئے۔ رازی نے زور دیا کہ نجات جامع تھی، بشمول غلامی سے جسمانی نجات، جابرانہ نظریے سے روحانی آزادی، اور باطل پر حق کا اخلاقی اثبات۔ طبری نے روایات ریکارڈ کیں کہ کس طرح فرعون نے بنی اسرائیل کو ظلم کیا اور کس طرح اللہ تعالیٰ نے انہیں نجات دی۔ دونوں روایات اس آیت کو استعمال کرتی ہیں تاکہ مظلوموں کو یاد دلائیں کہ اللہ تعالیٰ ان کی مدد کرتا ہے۔
115.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن الآية تُشير إلى نجاة الله لموسى وهارون وبني إسرائيل من اضطهاد فرعون بمعجزة انفلاق البحر. ويُفصِّل ابن كثير أبعاد الكرب واصفاً استعباد فرعون لبني إسرائيل وإكراههم على الأشغال الشاقة ومنهجية ذبح أطفالهم الذكور والاضطهاد الوحشي الذي لا يرحم. ويؤكد الرازي أن النجاة كانت شاملة: تحرراً جسدياً من العبودية وانعتاقاً روحياً من البيئة المفسدة وانتصاراً نفسياً بإهلاك مضطهديهم. ويُسجِّل الطبري روايات عديدة تصف الهروب المثير عبر البحر المنفلق وإغراق جيش فرعون المطارِد. ويُلاحِظ القرطبي أن وصف الكرب بـ"العظيم" يدل على شدته وشموله إذ طال كل جانب من جوانب حياة بني إسرائيل. ويؤكد العلماء الشيعة خاصةً أن الآية تُجسِّد العدل الإلهي والانتصار الحتمي للحق على الطغيان واهبةً الأمل لكل الأمم المضطهدة عبر التاريخ. ويوضح المفسر السني البيضاوي أن النجاة جاءت في أعقاب صبر طويل مُعلِّمةً أن التخليص الرباني يتطلب الثبات والتوكل. ويتفق التراثان على أن القصة تحمل دروساً خالدة في مواجهة الطغيان والثقة بالعون الإلهي وصدق اليقين بأن الله ينصر المستضعفين المظلومين على الطغاة المتجبرين.
115.layer1: Verse 115 continues: 'And We saved them and their people from the great affliction.' This verse describes one of the most dramatic rescues in prophetic history: the deliverance of Moses, Aaron, and the Children of Israel from the overwhelming oppression of Pharaoh and his regime. The Arabic term 'al-karb al-azim' (the great affliction or tremendous distress) captures in two words the totality of the suffering endured by the Israelites: centuries of enslavement, the slaughter of their infant sons, forced labour, humiliation, and spiritual oppression. Yet Allah describes saving them from all of this with the word 'najjayna' (We saved), a complete and decisive act of divine rescue. This verse is a powerful reminder that no matter how entrenched an oppressive system may appear, Allah has the power to overturn it entirely. The people of Moses were not saved by military power or political strategy alone; their deliverance came as a result of prophetic mission, sincere faith, and ultimately divine intervention at the Red Sea. For contemporary Muslims facing injustice or hardship, this verse carries the message that divine salvation is real, comprehensive, and available to those who hold firm to faith. The phrase 'and their people' is also significant: the rescue was not only for the prophets but extended to the entire believing community. Divine mercy operates collectively, encompassing all those connected to sincere faith and submission to Allah.
115.layer2: The rescue described in verse 115 is examined by classical scholars in connection with the broader narrative of Moses in the Quran. Imam Tabari in Jami al-Bayan identifies 'al-karb al-azim' as the totality of Pharaoh's oppression, which included the systematic killing of Israelite male children, forced servitude, and the denial of religious freedom. Tabari records traditions from the Companions and Tabi'un identifying the climactic moment of rescue as the parting of the Red Sea, when Pharaoh's army was destroyed and Israel was freed. Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim provides a rich cross-reference to Surah al-Baqarah and Surah Ta-Ha, where the same event is described in greater detail, noting that the deliverance of Moses and his people represents one of the greatest miracles documented in the Quran. Ibn Kathir emphasises that the divine rescue was both spiritual, in the sense of freeing people from the worship of Pharaoh, and physical, in the sense of liberating them from bondage. Imam Qurtubi in al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran notes that the use of 'al-karb al-azim' without further specification allows the verse to encompass all the dimensions of their suffering, and that Allah's rescue addressed all of these simultaneously. Al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb reflects that this verse, in the context of As-Saffat's broader pattern, serves to reassure the Prophet Muhammad that Allah's support for His messengers is total and guaranteed, ultimately encompassing both the individual prophet and their community of believers.
115.layer3: Modern Sunni scholars and thinkers reflect on verse 115 in the context of both its historical meaning and its enduring relevance. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran writes powerfully about the rescue of Moses and his people as a paradigm of divine justice. He argues that the Quran repeatedly invokes this narrative because the pattern of oppression, faithful endurance, and divine deliverance is not historically unique but recurs across time. For Qutb, the lesson for oppressed Muslim communities in the modern world is that faith and prophetic example are not passive consolations but active forces that draw upon divine power. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in al-Tafsir al-Munir draws out the communal dimension of verse 115, noting that the rescue of 'their people' alongside the prophets demonstrates that Allah's mercy extends to the community of believers who follow the prophets. Al-Zuhayli connects this to the Islamic principle of solidarity, where the fate of the community is tied to the righteousness of its leadership and the sincerity of its collective faith. Muhammad al-Sha'rawi emphasised in his popular lectures that 'al-karb al-azim', the great affliction, was not overcome by human means but by surrender to Allah, and that this surrender is always the key that unlocks divine rescue. In the modern world, where many Muslim communities face political, social, or spiritual pressures, this verse remains a living source of hope and the reminder that divine deliverance is not a relic of ancient history but an ever-present divine promise to the sincere.

concepts.title: Divine Support
concepts.coreInsight: 'We supported them' (nasarnahum) - Allah actively helped Musa and his people, showing that believers fight with divine backing, not just human strength.
concepts.whyItMatters: When you stand for truth, you don't stand alone. Allah's support (nasr) is with those who uphold His message, making the weaker party victorious.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'ہم نے ان کی مدد کی' - اللہ نے فعال طور پر موسیٰ اور ان کی قوم کی مدد کی، یہ دکھاتے ہوئے کہ مومن الہی حمایت سے لڑتے ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: جب آپ حق کے لیے کھڑے ہوتے ہیں، تو آپ اکیلے نہیں کھڑے ہوتے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'نصرناهم' - ساعد الله موسى وقومه بنشاط، مما يُظهر أن المؤمنين يقاتلون بدعم إلهي.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: عندما تقف من أجل الحق، لا تقف وحدك.

concepts.title: Ultimate Victory
concepts.coreInsight: 'So it was they who overcame' (fa-kanu hum al-ghalibun) - despite being enslaved and outnumbered, Bani Israel became the victors. Allah reverses worldly power dynamics.
concepts.whyItMatters: Victory belongs to those whom Allah supports, regardless of numbers, weapons, or worldly power. True strength comes from divine alignment.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'تو وہ غالب آئے' - غلام اور تعداد میں کم ہونے کے باوجود، بنی اسرائیل فاتح بن گئے۔ اللہ دنیاوی طاقت کی حرکیات کو بدل دیتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: فتح ان کی ہے جنہیں اللہ سہارا دیتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'فكانوا هم الغالبين' - على الرغم من العبودية والأقلية، أصبح بنو إسرائيل المنتصرين.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: النصر لمن يدعمهم الله.

concepts.title: Emphatic Identity
concepts.coreInsight: 'It was they' (hum) - the pronoun is emphatic, stressing that the weak and oppressed became the strong victors through Allah's intervention.
concepts.whyItMatters: Your current weakness doesn't determine your future. With Allah, the underdog story can become the victory story.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'یہ وہ تھے' - ضمیر تاکیدی ہے، اس بات پر زور دیتے ہوئے کہ کمزور اور مظلوم اللہ کی مداخلت سے مضبوط فاتح بن گئے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: آپ کی موجودہ کمزوری آپ کے مستقبل کا تعین نہیں کرتی۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: 'هم' - الضمير مؤكد، مشدداً على أن الضعفاء المضطهدين أصبحوا المنتصرين الأقوياء.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: ضعفك الحالي لا يحدد مستقبلك.

concepts.title: Justice Prevails
concepts.coreInsight: The verse affirms divine justice - oppressors may seem powerful temporarily, but Allah's justice ensures that righteousness ultimately prevails over tyranny.
concepts.whyItMatters: Never lose hope when facing injustice. History and divine promise show that truth outlasts falsehood, and justice overcomes oppression.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: آیت الہی انصاف کی تصدیق کرتی ہے - ظالم عارضی طور پر طاقتور نظر آ سکتے ہیں، لیکن اللہ کا انصاف یقینی بناتا ہے کہ صالحیت بالآخر ظلم پر غالب آتی ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ناانصافی کا سامنا کرتے وقت کبھی امید نہ ہاریں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تؤكد الآية العدالة الإلهية - قد يبدو الظالمون أقوياء مؤقتاً، لكن عدالة الله تضمن انتصار الحق.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: لا تفقد الأمل عند مواجهة الظلم.

116.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree that this verse describes Allah's support for Moses, Aaron, and the Israelites, resulting in their complete victory over Pharaoh. Ibn Kathir explains that the support included miraculous signs, divine protection, strengthening of hearts, and ultimately the destruction of their enemies and their own safe passage. Al-Razi emphasizes that the phrase 'they were the ones who overcame' indicates decisive and undeniable victory, not ambiguous or contested triumph. Tabari notes that the victory was achieved despite overwhelming material disadvantage, demonstrating that divine will determines outcomes more than worldly power. Qurtubi explains that divine support transforms the balance of power; the weak become strong and the strong become weak when Allah wills. Shia scholars particularly emphasize this verse as establishing a divine principle applicable throughout history: Allah supports those who stand for truth against tyranny, ensuring ultimate triumph. Sunni commentator al-Baydawi notes that the victory required both divine support and human effort, as Moses had to lead his people and take action in faith. Both traditions agree that the story provides crucial lessons about trusting divine support, persevering against oppression, and recognizing that ultimate victory belongs to those aligned with truth and justice. All schools teach that the verse encourages believers facing overwhelming challenges to maintain faith, knowing that divine support can reverse any situation and ensure triumph for those who remain steadfast in truth.
116.layer4_urdu: سنی اور شیعہ دونوں علماء اس بات پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ آیت موسیٰ علیہ السلام، ہارون علیہ السلام، اور بنی اسرائیل کے لیے اللہ تعالیٰ کی مدد کو بیان کرتی ہے، جس کے نتیجے میں فرعون پر ان کی مکمل فتح ہوئی۔ ابن کثیر نے وضاحت کی کہ مدد میں معجزانہ نشانات، الہی حفاظت، دلوں کو مضبوط کرنا، اور بالآخر ان کے دشمنوں کی تباہی اور ان کا اپنا محفوظ راستہ شامل تھا۔ رازی نے زور دیا کہ جملہ 'وہ وہ تھے جو غالب آئے' فیصلہ کن اور ناقابل تردید فتح کی نشاندہی کرتا ہے، مبہم یا متنازعہ فتح نہیں۔ طبری نے روایات ریکارڈ کیں کہ کس طرح اللہ تعالیٰ نے موسیٰ علیہ السلام اور ان کے لوگوں کی مدد کی۔ دونوں روایات اس آیت کو استعمال کرتی ہیں تاکہ مومنوں کو یاد دلائیں کہ اللہ تعالیٰ ان کی مدد کرتا ہے جو سچائی کے لیے کھڑے ہوتے ہیں۔
116.layer4_ar: يتفق العلماء من مختلف المذاهب الإسلامية على أن هذه الآية تصف نصر الله لموسى وهارون وبني إسرائيل وانتصارهم الساحق على فرعون وملئه. يشرح ابن كثير أن النصر شمل الآيات المعجزة، والحماية الإلهية، وتثبيت القلوب، وفي النهاية إهلاك الأعداء ونجاة المؤمنين. ويُبرز الرازي أن عبارة «فَكَانُوا هُمُ الْغَالِبِينَ» تدل على انتصار حاسم لا يحتمل إبهاماً أو جدلاً. ويُنوّه الطبري إلى أن النصر تحقق رغم التفاوت المادي الهائل، مما يُثبت أن الإرادة الإلهية تحسم نتائج الأحداث فوق الحسابات الدنيوية. ويُبيّن القرطبي أن النصر الإلهي يقلب موازين القوى؛ فيُقوّي الضعيف ويُضعف القوي متى شاء الله. ويُبرز علماء الشيعة بصفة خاصة هذه الآية باعتبارها تُؤسس مبدأً إلهياً سارياً عبر التاريخ: الله ينصر أهل الحق على الطغيان ويكفل نصرهم في النهاية. ويُلاحظ المفسر السني البيضاوي أن النصر اقتضى تأييداً إلهياً وجهداً بشرياً معاً، إذ قاد موسى قومه وأقدم على العمل بالإيمان. وتتفق جميع المذاهب على أن القصة تُوجب على المؤمنين الثقة بالنصر الإلهي، والثبات على المبدأ في مواجهة الظلم، واليقين بأن الكلمة الأخيرة لأهل الحق المتمسكين بدينهم.
116.layer1: Verse 116 of Surah As-Saffat declares that Allah granted Moses and Aaron His divine support, resulting in their ultimate victory over their enemies. The Arabic word 'nasarnahum' comes from the root n-s-r, meaning to give aid, support, and assistance. This verse comes within a sequence that enumerates the blessings Allah bestowed upon Moses and Aaron, beginning from verse 114. The historical context here is the confrontation between Moses and Pharaoh's magicians, and more broadly the entire struggle of the Children of Israel against the tyranny of Pharaoh and the Egyptian ruling class. Allah reminds the believers that true victory belongs only to those who stand with His prophets and uphold His message. The phrase 'fa-kanu humu al-ghalibun' — meaning 'so they became the victors' — carries a strong rhetorical emphasis through the use of the pronoun 'humu', which in Arabic signals exclusivity and decisiveness. This was not a partial or ambiguous outcome; it was complete and unmistakable triumph. For the Muslim believer, this verse teaches that when one sincerely aligns with divine guidance and trusts in Allah, victory is guaranteed even when all worldly signs point toward defeat. The story of Moses confronting the most powerful empire of his time with nothing but a staff and sincere faith stands as a timeless model of reliance on Allah. Every believer who stands for truth against seemingly impossible odds can draw deep comfort and inspiration from this declaration of divine support.
116.layer2: Imam Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan notes that the divine aid mentioned in this verse encompasses the full sweep of Allah's support for Moses and Aaron — from the initial confrontations with Pharaoh's court, to the miracles of the plagues, to the parting of the sea, and ultimately the destruction of Pharaoh's army. Tabari records narrations from the Companions and their successors emphasizing the totality of this victory: Pharaoh and his forces drowned while Moses and his people crossed safely, a decisive reversal that illustrated the irrevocable nature of divine assistance when it is granted. Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim explains the grammatical construction of 'fa-kanu humu al-ghalibun' in detail, pointing out that the definite form 'al-ghalibun' together with the separated pronoun 'humu' gives the sentence a meaning of total and exclusive victory — they and no one else were the true victors.
