concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اللہ اپنے رسولوں کو یقینی فتح (نصر) کا وعدہ کرتا ہے، صرف امید نہیں بلکہ الہی ضمانت۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: یہ یقین مخالفت کا سامنا کرنے والے مومنوں کو مضبوط کرتا ہے، یہ جانتے ہوئے کہ حتمی کامیابی الہی وعدہ ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يعد الله بنصر مؤكد لرسله، ليس مجرد أمل بل ضمان إلهي.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: هذا التأكيد يقوي المؤمنين الذين يواجهون المعارضة، عالمين أن النجاح النهائي موعود إلهيًا.

concepts.title: The Victorious
concepts.coreInsight: The definite article 'al-mansuroon' (THE victorious ones) emphasizes exclusivity - they alone will be aided.
concepts.whyItMatters: Victory belongs exclusively to those on Allah's path, not to the opposition regardless of their strength.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: قطعی سابقہ 'المنصورون' (فاتح) خصوصیت پر زور دیتا ہے - صرف انہیں مدد ملے گی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: فتح خاص طور پر ان لوگوں کی ہے جو اللہ کے راستے پر ہیں، نہ کہ مخالفین کی چاہے ان کی طاقت کتنی ہی ہو۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تؤكد أداة التعريف 'المنصورون' على الحصرية - هم وحدهم من سينالون العون.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: النصر ينتمي حصريًا لمن هم على طريق الله، وليس للمعارضة بغض النظر عن قوتهم.

concepts.title: Divine Support
concepts.coreInsight: Being 'mansur' means receiving Allah's active help and support, not just passive permission to succeed.
concepts.whyItMatters: Allah doesn't just allow victory; He actively intervenes to ensure His messengers prevail.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'منصور' ہونے کا مطلب اللہ کی فعال مدد اور حمایت حاصل کرنا ہے، نہ کہ صرف کامیابی کی غیر فعال اجازت۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ صرف فتح کی اجازت نہیں دیتا؛ وہ فعال طور پر مداخلت کرتا ہے تاکہ اس کے رسول غالب آئیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: أن تكون 'منصورًا' يعني تلقي مساعدة الله الفعالة ودعمه، وليس مجرد إذن سلبي بالنجاح.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: الله لا يسمح بالنصر فحسب؛ بل يتدخل بفعالية لضمان انتصار رسله.

172.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree on the fundamental interpretation of this verse as a divine promise of victory for the messengers. Ibn Kathir explains that this verse specifies the content of the preceding divine word: the messengers will be given victory (nasr) from Allah. Al-Tabari emphasizes the certainty of this promise, noting that what Allah has decreed must come to pass. Al-Qurtubi discusses the various ways this victory manifests—sometimes in the messenger's lifetime, sometimes posthumously through the spread of their message. Sunni exegete Fakhr al-Din al-Razi provides detailed analysis of the emphatic particles, showing that the grammar leaves no room for doubt about this promise. There is consensus that 'mansurun' (those given victory) is passive, indicating victory comes from Allah's support, not the messengers' own strength. Where traditions diverge is in scope and ongoing application. Shia scholars extend this promise to the Imams of Ahlul Bayt as the true successors and inheritors of the prophetic mission, arguing that divine support continues through them. They interpret Imam al-Mahdi's future advent as the ultimate fulfillment of this promise. Sunni commentators tend to limit the verse more strictly to the original prophets. However, both traditions agree that the verse provides assurance that truth will ultimately triumph, making it a source of hope and resilience for believers facing opposition in any era.
172.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی علماء دونوں اس آیت کی بنیادی تشریح پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ رسولوں کے لیے فتح کا الہٰی وعدہ ہے۔ ابن کثیر وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ یہ آیت پہلے الہٰی کلام کا مضمون بیان کرتی ہے: رسولوں کو اللہ کی طرف سے فتح (نصر) دی جائے گی۔ طبری اس وعدے کی یقینی نوعیت پر زور دیتے ہیں، نوٹ کرتے ہوئے کہ جو اللہ نے مقرر کیا ہے وہ پورا ہونا ضروری ہے۔ قرطبی مختلف طریقوں پر بحث کرتے ہیں جن سے یہ فتح ظاہر ہوتی ہے، کبھی رسول کی زندگی میں، کبھی مرنے کے بعد ان کے پیغام کے پھیلاؤ کے ذریعے۔ سنی مفسر فخر الدین رازی تاکیدی الفاظ کا تفصیلی تجزیہ فراہم کرتے ہیں، ظاہر کرتے ہوئے کہ گرامر اس وعدے کے بارے میں کوئی شک نہیں چھوڑتی۔ اس بات پر اتفاق ہے کہ 'منصورون' (جن کی مدد کی جائے) مبنی برائے مجہول ہے، ظاہر کرتا ہے کہ فتح اللہ کی مدد سے آتی ہے، رسولوں کی اپنی طاقت سے نہیں۔ جہاں روایات مختلف ہیں وہ دائرہ کار اور جاری اطلاق میں ہے۔ شیعہ علماء اس وعدے کو اہل بیت کے ائمہ تک بڑھاتے ہیں بطور نبوی مشن کے حقیقی جانشین اور وارث، دلیل دیتے ہوئے کہ الہٰی مدد ان کے ذریعے جاری رہتی ہے۔ سنی مفسرین آیت کو زیادہ سختی سے اصل انبیاء تک محدود رکھتے ہیں۔
172.layer4_ar: يتفق التراثان الشيعي والسني اتفاقاً جوهرياً على معنى هذه الآية بوصفها وعداً إلهياً بنصرة الرسل. ويُبيِّن ابن كثير أن هذه الآية تُحدِّد مضمون الكلمة الإلهية في الآية السابقة: الرسل سيُمنحون النصر من الله. ويُشدِّد الطبري على يقين هذا الوعد، إذ ما قضى به الله فلا بد أن يتحقق. ويستعرض القرطبي الصور المختلفة التي يتجلى فيها هذا الانتصار؛ أحياناً في حياة الرسول ذاته، وأحياناً بعد رحيله بانتشار رسالته. ويُقدِّم المفسر السني فخر الدين الرازي تحليلاً مستفيضاً لأدوات التوكيد، مُبيِّناً أن قواعد اللغة لا تترك مجالاً للشك في هذا الوعد. ويتفق التراثان على أن «مَنصورون» اسم مفعول يُشير إلى أن النصر يأتي من عند الله لا من قوة الرسل الذاتية. وموضع الاختلاف يكمن في النطاق والتطبيق الموسَّع؛ فالعلماء الشيعة يمدُّون هذا الوعد ليشمل أئمة أهل البيت بوصفهم الخلفاء الحقيقيين والورثة الشرعيين للرسالة النبوية، ويعتبرون مجيء الإمام المهدي الوفاء الأكمل بهذا الوعد. في المقابل يميل المفسرون السنة إلى حصر الوعد في الأنبياء الأصليين دون تمديده. غير أن التراثين يتفقان في المآل على أن الآية تُؤكِّد انتصار الحق على الباطل، مما يجعلها مصدر أمل وصمود للمؤمنين في مواجهة المعارضة في كل زمان ومكان.
172.layer1: Verse 172 continues the divine promise begun in verse 171: 'Indeed, it is they who will be made victorious.' The Arabic 'innahum lahum al-mansurun' uses strong emphasis through the particle 'inna' (indeed) and the doubled pronoun 'lahum' (it is they), making the statement emphatic and exclusive. The word 'al-mansurun' comes from the root 'nasara' meaning to help, support, and grant victory. This is not a mere possibility but a definitive divine guarantee. The Messengers of Allah are those whom Allah Himself will support with His divine aid, sending angels, arranging worldly circumstances, and ultimately ensuring their mission succeeds. This verse is a direct comfort to Prophet Muhammad who, surrounded by mockers and enemies in Mecca, needed this assurance that his patient perseverance would not be in vain. For the broader Muslim community, this verse teaches that genuine divine support (nasr) is tied to fulfilling the prophetic mission — calling to Allah, maintaining moral integrity, and persisting through opposition. The prophetic model shows that divine victory does not always come immediately; Ibrahim waited decades, Yusuf endured years of imprisonment, and Musa faced Pharaoh with nothing but a staff. Yet all were ultimately made victorious. The believer learns that true support from Allah comes to those who remain committed to truth even when the world appears to be against them. This verse should be memorised and reflected upon deeply during times of personal or communal hardship.
172.layer2: Ibn Kathir explains that verse 172 is a direct elaboration of the divine decree established in verse 171. The statement 'innahum lahum al-mansurun' is rendered by Ibn Kathir as meaning that the Messengers — and by extension their genuine followers — are those guaranteed Allah's support. He cites the hadith reported in Sahih al-Bukhari in which the Prophet described that Allah the Almighty said: 'I shall certainly support My servants who were sent with My message.' Ibn Kathir notes that this verse was contextualised by the early Muslim community as applying not just to the Prophets themselves but to the inheritors of the prophetic mission in every age, namely the scholars, the righteous, and all sincere believers. Tabari's Jami al-Bayan analyses the grammatical structure of 'lahum al-mansurun,' observing that the placement of 'lahum' before 'al-mansurun' in Arabic grammar creates what is called a restriction (hasr or qasr), meaning it is specifically and exclusively they who are designated for this divine support. Imam Qurtubi connects this verse to the principle that divine victory (nasr) sometimes comes in the form of worldly triumph, and sometimes in the form of spiritual elevation and the perpetuation of one's legacy — as seen in the case of Prophets like Yahya and Zakariyya who were martyred yet whose message endured. The Salaf understood this verse as one of the foundational Quranic texts affirming the doctrine of divine faithfulness to those who carry His message.
172.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir contextualises verse 172 within the broader Quranic doctrine of divine support, referencing parallel verses such as Surah Hajj (22:40): 'And Allah is Most Powerful to grant victory.' Al-Zuhayli emphasises that 'al-mansurun' encompasses victory at multiple levels: the internal victory of certainty and spiritual peace, the social victory of having one's message preserved and transmitted through generations, and the ultimate victory of vindication in the Hereafter. Sheikh Muhammad al-Sha'rawi, the beloved Egyptian scholar, observed that this verse reveals an important spiritual principle — Allah's support comes to those who fulfil the conditions of sincere servitude, not merely to those who claim prophetic inheritance. The Messengers earned this designation through total devotion, patience, and trust in Allah alone. Sayyid Qutb notes in Fi Zilal al-Quran that this verse was the theological anchor for generations of Muslims who faced persecution — from the companions of the early Meccan period to Muslims in modern times who have faced marginalisation. Contemporary Islamic scholarship continues to draw on this verse to argue that the ultimate measure of success in Islam is not political power or numerical strength but faithfulness to the divine mission. The verse also carries an implicit challenge to believers today: to ask themselves whether they are genuinely aligned with the prophetic mission so that they may be counted among those whom Allah's promise covers.

concepts.title: Divine Army
concepts.coreInsight: Allah describes believers and angels as 'Our soldiers' (junduna), emphasizing they fight under divine command.
concepts.whyItMatters: Seeing ourselves as Allah's soldiers transforms our struggles into sacred missions with guaranteed ultimate success.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اللہ مومنوں اور فرشتوں کو 'ہماری فوج' (جندنا) کے طور پر بیان کرتا ہے، زور دیتے ہوئے کہ وہ الہی حکم کے تحت لڑتے ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اپنے آپ کو اللہ کی فوج کے طور پر دیکھنا ہماری جدوجہد کو مقدس مشنوں میں تبدیل کرتا ہے جس میں حتمی کامیابی کی ضمانت ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يصف الله المؤمنين والملائكة بـ'جندنا'، مؤكدًا أنهم يقاتلون تحت الأمر الإلهي.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: رؤية أنفسنا كجنود الله تحول صراعاتنا إلى مهام مقدسة مع ضمان النجاح النهائي.

concepts.title: Ultimate Triumph
concepts.coreInsight: The term 'ghaliboon' (those who overcome) promises not just victory but dominance and superiority.
concepts.whyItMatters: Truth will not merely survive but will ultimately prevail and dominate over falsehood.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اصطلاح 'غالبون' (غالب آنے والے) صرف فتح کا نہیں بلکہ غلبہ اور برتری کا وعدہ کرتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: حق صرف زندہ نہیں رہے گا بلکہ بالآخر باطل پر غالب اور حاوی ہوگا۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يعد مصطلح 'الغالبون' ليس فقط بالنصر بل بالهيمنة والتفوق.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: الحق لن ينجو فحسب بل سينتصر في النهاية ويسود على الباطل.

concepts.title: Parallel Promise
concepts.coreInsight: This verse parallels the previous one, reinforcing the promise through repetition with slightly different terminology.
concepts.whyItMatters: Divine repetition emphasizes certainty; when Allah repeats a promise, it's to remove all doubt from our hearts.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: یہ آیت پچھلی آیت کے متوازی ہے، تھوڑی مختلف اصطلاحات کے ساتھ تکرار کے ذریعے وعدے کو تقویت دیتی ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: الہی تکرار یقین پر زور دیتی ہے؛ جب اللہ وعدہ دہراتا ہے، تو یہ ہمارے دلوں سے تمام شک کو دور کرنے کے لیے ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: توازي هذه الآية السابقة، معززة الوعد من خلال التكرار بمصطلحات مختلفة قليلاً.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: التكرار الإلهي يؤكد اليقين؛ عندما يكرر الله وعدًا، فذلك لإزالة كل شك من قلوبنا.

173.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree on the fundamental meaning of this verse as a divine promise that Allah's army will ultimately prevail. Ibn Kathir explains that 'junduna' (Our soldiers) refers to the believers and the angels who support them, and that their ultimate victory is guaranteed by divine decree. Al-Tabari provides similar interpretation, noting that this promise was fulfilled in the Prophet's lifetime through victories like Badr and the conquest of Mecca, and continues to be fulfilled through the spread of Islam. Al-Qurtubi emphasizes that being part of Allah's army requires genuine faith and righteous action, not mere lip service. Sunni exegete Fakhr al-Din al-Razi discusses the comprehensiveness of the term 'jund,' noting that it includes all forces Allah uses to support His cause. There is consensus across both traditions that this verse provides assurance to believers facing opposition. Where interpretations diverge is in identifying who constitutes Allah's army in the post-prophetic era. Shia scholars emphasize that true membership in Allah's jund requires following the divinely appointed Imams, and that the ultimate fulfillment of this promise will come through Imam al-Mahdi who will lead the final victory of truth over falsehood. Sunni commentators have broader criteria for who constitutes Allah's army, generally including all sincere Muslims fighting in legitimate causes. However, both traditions agree that the verse promises ultimate triumph for those truly aligned with divine purpose, providing hope and motivation for believers throughout history.
173.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی علماء دونوں اس آیت کے بنیادی معنی پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ الہٰی وعدہ ہے کہ اللہ کا لشکر بالآخر غالب آئے گا۔ ابن کثیر وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ 'جُنْدُنَا' (ہمارے لشکر) سے مراد مومنین اور فرشتے ہیں جو ان کی مدد کرتے ہیں، اور ان کی حتمی فتح الہٰی فرمان سے یقینی ہے۔ طبری اسی طرح کی تشریح فراہم کرتے ہیں، نوٹ کرتے ہوئے کہ یہ وعدہ نبی کی زندگی میں بدر اور فتح مکہ جیسی فتوحات کے ذریعے پورا ہوا، اور اسلام کے پھیلاؤ کے ذریعے جاری رہتا ہے۔ قرطبی زور دیتے ہیں کہ اللہ کے لشکر کا حصہ بننے کے لیے حقیقی ایمان اور نیک عمل کی ضرورت ہے، محض زبانی دعوے کی نہیں۔ سنی مفسر فخر الدین رازی لفظ 'جُنْد' کی وسعت پر بحث کرتے ہیں، نوٹ کرتے ہوئے کہ اس میں تمام قوتیں شامل ہیں جنہیں اللہ اپنے مقصد کی مدد کے لیے استعمال کرتا ہے۔ دونوں روایات میں اتفاق ہے کہ یہ آیت مخالفت کا سامنا کرنے والے مومنین کو یقین دہانی فراہم کرتی ہے۔ جہاں تشریحات مختلف ہیں وہ یہ ہے کہ نبوی دور کے بعد کون اللہ کے لشکر کو تشکیل دیتا ہے۔ شیعہ علماء زور دیتے ہیں کہ اللہ کے جُنْد میں حقیقی رکنیت الہٰی طور پر مقرر کردہ ائمہ کی پیروی کی ضرورت ہے۔
173.layer4_ar: يتفق التراثان الشيعي والسني اتفاقاً جوهرياً على معنى هذه الآية بوصفها وعداً إلهياً بأن جند الله سينتصر في نهاية المطاف. ويُبيِّن ابن كثير أن «جُندَنَا» يشمل المؤمنين والملائكة الذين يُسندونهم، وأن انتصارهم الأخير مكفول بالقضاء الإلهي. ويُقدِّم الطبري تفسيراً مماثلاً، مُلاحِظاً أن هذا الوعد تجلى في انتصارات كبدر وفتح مكة، وما زال يتحقق بانتشار الإسلام. ويُشدِّد القرطبي على أن الانتساب إلى جند الله يستلزم إيماناً أصيلاً وعملاً صالحاً لا مجرد ادعاء. ويُناقش المفسر السني فخر الدين الرازي شمولية معنى «جُند»، مُلاحِظاً أنه يستوعب جميع القوى التي يُسخِّرها الله لمساندة قضيته. ويتفق التراثان على أن الآية تُوفِّر تطمينة للمؤمنين الذين يواجهون المعارضة. وموضع الاختلاف يكمن في تحديد هوية جند الله في مرحلة ما بعد النبوة؛ فالعلماء الشيعة يُشدِّدون على أن الانتساب الحقيقي لجنده يستلزم اتباع أئمة أهل البيت المعيَّنين بالأمر الإلهي، مؤكِّدين أن الوفاء الأخير بهذا الوعد سيكون على يد الإمام المهدي الذي سيقود انتصار الحق النهائي على الباطل. في المقابل يضع المفسرون السنة معايير أوسع لتحديد جند الله، إذ يشملون في العموم كل المسلمين المخلصين الساعين في أسباب مشروعة. غير أن التراثين يتفقان على أن الآية تَعِد بالانتصار الأخير لمن انحاز فعلاً إلى المشيئة الإلهية، مما يُوفِّر الأمل والدافعية للمؤمنين في كل عصر ومصر.
173.layer1: Verse 173 declares: 'And indeed, it is Our host who will be the victors.' The term 'jundana' (Our host or Our army) is a deeply significant expression, describing the collective body of believers as soldiers in Allah's cause. The word 'jund' in Arabic refers to an organised military force, but in the Quranic usage it takes on a spiritual dimension — the host of Allah is composed of those who fight in His cause with faith, sincerity, and adherence to His guidance. The verse asserts that this divine army will be 'al-ghalibun' — the ones who prevail or overcome. The root 'ghalaba' means to dominate, overcome, or surpass. Together, 'lahum al-ghalibun' forms another emphatic construction similar to verse 172, underscoring that this victory is not contingent on numbers or material strength but on divine backing. Historically, this was proven at the Battle of Badr where 313 Muslims overcame an army three times their size; at the conquest of Mecca when the city that expelled the Prophet received him as its conqueror; and across centuries of Islamic civilisation. The verse reminds every Muslim that membership in the 'host of Allah' carries both privilege and responsibility. One belongs to this host through sincere faith, righteous conduct, and active participation in calling people to goodness. It is a verse that should inspire collective identity and solidarity among believers, reminding them that they are part of something larger than individual struggles — a divinely supported global community with a guaranteed ultimate victory.
173.layer2: Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan explains that 'jundana' in verse 173 refers to the believers collectively, the followers of the Messengers in every age, not merely the Messengers themselves. He transmits the opinion of scholars of the Salaf that this expression encompasses all sincere believers who align themselves with the prophetic cause. Ibn Kathir affirms this reading, stating that 'Our host' refers to the believers, the faithful followers of the Messengers — and that their ultimate predominance is guaranteed by this Quranic decree. Ibn Kathir also cites the historical fulfilment of this promise: the early Muslims who were a persecuted minority became the leading civilisation of their era, a proof he saw as validating the divine promise of verse 173. Imam Qurtubi draws an important legal and theological distinction here: he notes that the promise of victory is to 'Our host' — meaning those who are genuinely in the cause of Allah — and not simply to any group that claims Islamic identity. Qurtubi emphasises that the prerequisite for belonging to the host of Allah is sincere faith combined with righteous action. This understanding prevented the Salaf from interpreting the verse as an unconditional guarantee regardless of one's moral and spiritual state. The classical scholars also noted that 'al-ghalibun' (the victors) does not specify the timeline or the form of victory, leaving open that divine triumph may manifest in this world, in the afterlife, or in both, as befits each situation.
173.layer3: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran writes with particular eloquence about verse 173, arguing that this verse establishes a permanent Quranic principle — that truth, when it has genuine bearers, ultimately prevails over falsehood. Qutb connects this to his broader thesis that Islam, as a complete system, carries within it the seeds of its own victory because it aligns with the nature of human beings (fitra) and the laws of the universe. Wahbah al-Zuhayli observes that modern readers sometimes interpret the 'host of Allah' narrowly, but the Quranic usage is comprehensive — it includes scholars, teachers, parents raising righteous children, writers, and every believer contributing sincerely to the preservation and spread of divine guidance. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, in his teaching circles on the Quran, noted that verse 173 should infuse the believer with collective confidence rather than despair at the apparent strength of opposing forces. He drew attention to the lesson from Surah Al-Maidah (5:56) — 'it is the party of Allah who will be the successful' — as a parallel affirmation that membership in the divine side guarantees ultimate success. Contemporary Muslim scholars also note that this verse has shaped Islamic historical consciousness, providing the psychological and theological framework that enabled Muslim communities to rebuild and revive after periods of decline and defeat, trusting that the promise of divine victory remains operative for every generation that sincerely fulfils the conditions of faith and righteous striving.

concepts.title: Strategic Withdrawal
concepts.coreInsight: Allah commands the Prophet to turn away from opponents temporarily, showing that engagement isn't always immediate.
concepts.whyItMatters: Sometimes wisdom lies in strategic patience rather than immediate confrontation; timing is divine.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اللہ نبی کو حکم دیتا ہے کہ مخالفین سے عارضی طور پر منہ موڑ لیں، ظاہر کرتے ہوئے کہ مشغولیت ہمیشہ فوری نہیں ہوتی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: بعض اوقات حکمت فوری تصادم کی بجائے حکمت عملی سے صبر میں ہے؛ وقت الہی ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يأمر الله النبي بالابتعاد عن الخصوم مؤقتًا، مظهرًا أن المواجهة ليست دائمًا فورية.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: أحيانًا تكمن الحكمة في الصبر الاستراتيجي بدلاً من المواجهة الفورية؛ التوقيت إلهي.

concepts.title: Appointed Time
concepts.coreInsight: The phrase 'hatta heen' (until a time) indicates a specific moment determined by Allah when matters will be resolved.
concepts.whyItMatters: Everything happens according to divine timing; we must trust Allah's schedule even when results seem delayed.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: جملہ 'حتی حین' (ایک وقت تک) ایک مخصوص لمحے کی نشاندہی کرتا ہے جو اللہ نے طے کیا ہے جب معاملات حل ہوں گے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: سب کچھ الہی وقت کے مطابق ہوتا ہے؛ ہمیں اللہ کے شیڈول پر بھروسہ کرنا چاہیے چاہے نتائج میں تاخیر معلوم ہو۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تشير عبارة 'حتى حين' إلى لحظة محددة قررها الله عندما ستُحل الأمور.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: كل شيء يحدث وفقًا للتوقيت الإلهي؛ يجب أن نثق بجدول الله حتى عندما تبدو النتائج متأخرة.

concepts.title: Prophetic Patience
concepts.coreInsight: This command to the Prophet models patience for all believers facing opposition or delayed justice.
concepts.whyItMatters: If even the Prophet was told to wait, our patience during trials is part of the divine plan.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: نبی کو یہ حکم تمام مومنوں کے لیے صبر کا نمونہ ہے جو مخالفت یا تاخیر سے انصاف کا سامنا کر رہے ہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اگر نبی کو بھی انتظار کرنے کو کہا گیا، تو آزمائشوں کے دوران ہمارا صبر الہی منصوبے کا حصہ ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: هذا الأمر للنبي يُنمذج الصبر لجميع المؤمنين الذين يواجهون معارضة أو عدالة متأخرة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: إذا قيل حتى للنبي أن ينتظر، فصبرنا خلال المحن جزء من الخطة الإلهية.

174.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree on the basic interpretation of this verse as a command to the Prophet to temporarily disengage from direct confrontation with the hostile Quraysh. Ibn Kathir explains that this was revealed in Mecca when Muslims were weak, commanding the Prophet to be patient and leave judgment to Allah. Al-Tabari notes that 'hatta hin' (until a time) could refer to the conquest of Mecca, the Battle of Badr, or the Day of Judgment. Al-Qurtubi emphasizes that this verse taught strategic patience, not abandonment of the mission. There is consensus that the verse provided psychological comfort to the Prophet during persecution. Sunni exegete Fakhr al-Din al-Razi discusses the wisdom of this command in preserving the nascent Muslim community from premature confrontation. Where traditions differ is in broader theological application. Shia scholars connect this verse to the principle of taqiyyah (precautionary dissimulation) practiced by the Imams when facing overwhelming oppression, arguing that strategic withdrawal to preserve the community and mission is a legitimate practice established by Quranic precedent. They point to Imam Ali's strategic patience after the Prophet's death as an example. Most Sunni scholars acknowledge the temporary nature of this command without developing a broader doctrine of taqiyyah. However, both traditions agree that the verse teaches wisdom in choosing when to confront opposition and when to exercise strategic patience, trusting in divine timing for ultimate justice.
174.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی علماء دونوں اس آیت کی تشریح پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ حکمت عملی کے صبر اور براہ راست مقابلے سے علیحدگی کا حکم ہے۔ ابن کثیر وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ یہ مکہ میں نازل ہوئی جب مسلمان کمزور تھے، نبی کو حکم دیتے ہوئے کہ صبر کریں اور فیصلہ اللہ پر چھوڑ دیں۔ طبری نوٹ کرتے ہیں کہ 'حَتّٰی حِیْن' (ایک وقت تک) فتح مکہ، جنگ بدر، یا قیامت کی طرف اشارہ ہو سکتا ہے۔ قرطبی زور دیتے ہیں کہ اس آیت نے حکمت عملی کے صبر کو سکھایا، مشن کو ترک کرنا نہیں۔ دونوں روایات میں اتفاق ہے کہ آیت نے ظلم کے دوران نبی کو نفسیاتی سکون فراہم کیا۔ جہاں روایات قدرے مختلف ہیں وہ وسیع تر نظریاتی اطلاق میں ہے: شیعہ علماء اس آیت کو تقیہ (احتیاطی چھپاؤ) کے اصول سے جوڑتے ہیں جو ائمہ نے بھاری ظلم کا سامنا کرتے وقت استعمال کیا، دلیل دیتے ہوئے کہ برادری اور مشن کو محفوظ رکھنے کے لیے حکمت عملی کے مطابق پیچھے ہٹنا قرآنی نظیر سے قائم شدہ جائز عمل ہے۔
174.layer4_ar: يتفق التراثان الشيعي والسني اتفاقاً جوهرياً على المعنى الأساسي لهذه الآية بوصفها أمراً للنبي بالانسحاب المؤقت عن المواجهة المباشرة مع قريش المتعنتة. ويُبيِّن ابن كثير أن هذا نزل في مكة حين كان المسلمون ضعافاً، فأُمر النبي بالصبر وترك الحكم لله. ويُلاحِظ الطبري أن «حَتَّى حِينٍ» قد يُراد به فتح مكة أو غزوة بدر أو يوم القيامة. ويُشدِّد القرطبي على أن الآية علَّمت الصبر الاستراتيجي لا التخلي عن الرسالة. ويستعرض المفسر السني فخر الدين الرازي حكمة هذا التوجيه في صون المجتمع الإسلامي الناشئ من المواجهة المبكرة. وموضع الاختلاف يكمن في التطبيق العقدي الأوسع؛ إذ يربط العلماء الشيعة هذه الآية بمبدأ التقية الذي مارسه الأئمة في مواجهة الطغيان الساحق، مُقرِّرين أن الانسحاب الاستراتيجي لصون الجماعة والرسالة ممارسة مشروعة راسخة في سابقة قرآنية. ويستشهدون بصبر الإمام علي الاستراتيجي إثر وفاة النبي مثالاً على ذلك. وأكثر علماء السنة لا يُطوِّرون من هذا النص عقيدة واسعة في التقية. غير أن التراثين يتفقان على أن الآية تُعلِّم الحكمة في اختيار أوقات مواجهة المعارضة وأوقات الصبر الاستراتيجي، مع الثقة بالتوقيت الإلهي في إجراء العدل الأخير.
174.layer1: Verse 174 brings a direct address to Prophet Muhammad: 'So turn away from them for a while.' The command 'fatawalla anhum' uses the root 'tawalla' which means to turn away, withdraw, or avert oneself. The phrase 'hatta hin' means 'until a time' or 'for a while,' indicating a temporary posture rather than permanent abandonment. Allah is instructing the Prophet to temporarily withdraw from active confrontation with the Meccan polytheists — not to abandon them spiritually, but to adopt a strategic patience while the divine plan unfolds. This command is notable because it reveals an important Islamic principle: not every situation calls for immediate confrontation. Wisdom sometimes dictates stepping back, enduring with patience, and waiting for the right moment. The Prophet was not being told to give up dawah (calling to Islam) but rather to manage his engagement prudently during a particularly intense phase of persecution. This verse was likely revealed when the hostility of the Meccan leadership was at a peak, and the believers were in a position of relative weakness. The word 'hin' (a while) is deliberately vague, leaving the duration to divine wisdom rather than human calculation. For Muslims today, this verse models a spiritually mature form of patience — continuing one's mission in heart while pausing direct confrontation when circumstances make it unwise or counter-productive. It teaches that withdrawal when necessary is not defeat but tactical wisdom guided by trust in Allah's timing.
174.layer2: Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim explains the command in verse 174 as meaning: 'Bear their annoyance with patience and wait until an appointed time, when We shall cause you to prevail and will grant you victory.' He connects this verse to the broader Meccan context in which the Prophet faced intense opposition, mockery, and persecution, and understands the divine command as a merciful instruction to the Prophet to preserve his energy and spiritual state while awaiting Allah's promised support. Tabari in Jami al-Bayan records that several scholars of the early Muslim community understood 'hatta hin' as referring specifically to the period before the battles and the eventual triumph at Mecca — the 'time' being the divinely determined moment when the believers would be permitted to respond to persecution with strength. The verse relates to what Tabari discusses as the principle of istimhal (patience while waiting for the divinely decreed moment of relief). Imam Qurtubi notes that this verse is part of a sequence of verses that were later 'contextually superseded' in their specific application by verses permitting defensive warfare (qital), though the principle of strategic patience remains permanently valid. Qurtubi draws on this verse to articulate the fiqh principle that the mode of dawah must adapt to circumstances and that wisdom (hikmah) is an essential component of the prophetic mission alongside clarity and courage. The Salaf saw this verse as modelling the Prophet's moral refinement — his ability to maintain composure and trust in Allah even when commanded to step back temporarily.
174.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir reflects on verse 174 as establishing a Quranic principle of strategic disengagement — the idea that the believer working for Islam must have the wisdom to know when to advance, when to engage, and when to momentarily withdraw. Al-Zuhayli notes that this verse does not imply passivity or defeatism but rather models prophetic wisdom in managing the pace of confrontation with falsehood. He cites the Prophetic biography as the living commentary on this verse: the Prophet endured thirteen years in Mecca with measured patience before the conditions for active resistance were established. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran interprets this command as a divine gift of reassurance — Allah is essentially telling the Prophet: the outcome is in Our hands, you do not need to force the moment; trust in Our timing. This reading transforms 'turn away for a while' from a seeming retreat into an act of profound faith and trust in divine orchestration. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen in his commentary circles emphasised that verse 174 teaches believers the virtue of 'tawakkul' (reliance on Allah) in the practical sense — not abandoning effort, but releasing the anxiety of needing to control outcomes. Contemporary Islamic scholars apply this verse to contexts where Muslim minorities face hostility, counselling a combination of principled engagement, wise avoidance of unnecessary conflict, and patient confidence in the ultimate rightness of their position. The verse ultimately calls every Muslim to develop the spiritual maturity to trust Allah's timing even when the human impulse is to act urgently.

concepts.title: Witness Justice
concepts.coreInsight: The Prophet is told to observe ('absir') what will happen to opponents - a promise he'll witness their downfall.
concepts.whyItMatters: Believers will see divine justice manifest; patience is rewarded with witnessing truth prevail.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: نبی کو کہا گیا ہے کہ مشاہدہ کریں ('ابصر') کہ مخالفین کو کیا ہوگا - ایک وعدہ کہ وہ ان کے زوال کے گواہ ہوں گے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: مومن الہی انصاف کو ظاہر ہوتے دیکھیں گے؛ صبر کا بدلہ حق کے غالب آنے کے گواہ بننے سے ملتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يُخبر النبي بمراقبة ('أبصر') ما سيحدث للخصوم - وعد بأنه سيشهد سقوطهم.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: سيرى المؤمنون العدالة الإلهية تتجلى؛ الصبر يُكافأ بمشاهدة الحق ينتصر.

concepts.title: Mutual Seeing
concepts.coreInsight: The wordplay on 'see' emphasizes both the Prophet seeing their fate and them seeing their error too late.
concepts.whyItMatters: Truth will be made visible to all; deniers will eventually see what believers saw all along.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'دیکھنے' پر لفظی کھیل نبی کے ان کی قسمت دیکھنے اور ان کے اپنی غلطی کو بہت دیر سے دیکھنے دونوں پر زور دیتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: حق سب کے لیے مرئی بنایا جائے گا؛ انکار کرنے والے بالآخر وہ دیکھیں گے جو مومنوں نے پہلے سے دیکھا۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: التلاعب بكلمة 'رؤية' يؤكد على النبي الذي يرى مصيرهم ورؤيتهم لخطئهم متأخرًا جدًا.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: سيُجعل الحق مرئيًا للجميع؛ سيرى المنكرون في النهاية ما رآه المؤمنون طوال الوقت.

concepts.title: Inevitability
concepts.coreInsight: The certainty particle 'sawfa' (going to) emphasizes the inevitable future realization of truth.
concepts.whyItMatters: Divine justice may be delayed but is never denied; what's promised will certainly come.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: یقینی ذرہ 'سوف' (ہونے والا) حق کی ناگزیر مستقبل کی تحقق پر زور دیتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: الہی انصاف میں تاخیر ہو سکتی ہے لیکن کبھی انکار نہیں؛ جو وعدہ کیا گیا وہ یقیناً آئے گا۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تؤكد أداة التأكيد 'سوف' على التحقق المستقبلي الحتمي للحقيقة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: قد تتأخر العدالة الإلهية لكنها لا تُنكر أبدًا؛ ما وُعد به سيأتي بالتأكيد.

175.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree on the fundamental interpretation of this verse as a command to observe the enemies and a promise that they will face consequences. Ibn Kathir explains that the Prophet is commanded to observe what will befall them as punishment for their rejection of truth. Al-Tabari notes that this was fulfilled at Badr where many Quraysh leaders died, and at the conquest of Mecca where the Prophet's former enemies witnessed his triumph. Al-Qurtubi emphasizes the certainty of the promise 'they will see,' indicating inevitable punishment. Sunni exegete Fakhr al-Din al-Razi discusses the rhetorical power of the repetition of 'seeing' in creating anticipation and warning. There is consensus across both traditions that the verse provides comfort to believers facing persecution and warns oppressors of coming accountability. Where traditions differ slightly is in emphasis and extended application. Shia scholars tend to emphasize the spiritual dimension of basira (insight) more deeply, connecting it to the wisdom taught by the Ahlul Bayt about reading divine patterns in history. They also extend the principle to the ultimate vindication of the Imams whose opponents eventually faced defeat or disgrace. Sunni commentators focus more exclusively on the original historical context of the Quraysh facing defeat at Badr and Mecca. However, both traditions agree that the verse establishes that divine justice will manifest clearly, making the current suffering of the righteous temporary while the apparent triumph of the wicked is illusory.
175.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی علماء دونوں اس آیت کی بنیادی تشریح پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ دشمنوں کا مشاہدہ کرنے کا حکم اور ایک وعدہ ہے کہ وہ نتائج کا سامنا کریں گے۔ ابن کثیر وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ نبی کو حکم دیا گیا ہے کہ مشاہدہ کریں کہ ان پر حق کو مسترد کرنے کی سزا کے طور پر کیا آئے گی۔ طبری نوٹ کرتے ہیں کہ یہ بدر میں پورا ہوا جہاں بہت سے قریش رہنما مارے گئے، اور فتح مکہ میں جہاں نبی کے سابقہ دشمنوں نے ان کی فتح کا مشاہدہ کیا۔ قرطبی وعدے 'وہ دیکھیں گے' کی یقینی نوعیت پر زور دیتے ہیں، ناگزیر سزا کی نشاندہی کرتے ہوئے۔ سنی مفسر فخر الدین رازی 'دیکھنے' کے اعادہ کی بلاغت کی طاقت پر بحث کرتے ہیں، توقع اور انتباہ پیدا کرنے میں۔ دونوں روایات میں اتفاق ہے کہ آیت ظلم کا سامنا کرنے والے مومنین کو سکون فراہم کرتی ہے اور ظالموں کو آنے والی جوابدہی کی خبردار کرتی ہے۔
175.layer4_ar: يتفق التراثان الشيعي والسني اتفاقاً جوهرياً على المعنى الأساسي للآية بوصفها أمراً للنبي بمراقبة أعدائه ووعداً بأنهم سيواجهون عواقب معارضتهم. ويُبيِّن ابن كثير أن النبي مأمور بمراقبة ما سيُصيبهم من عذاب جزاء رفضهم الحق. ويُلاحِظ الطبري أن هذا الوعد تجلَّى في بدر حيث هلك كثير من رؤوس قريش، وفي فتح مكة حيث شهد أعداء النبي انتصار ما أرادوا له الإخفاق. ويُشدِّد القرطبي على يقين الوعيد «سَوف يُبصرون» ودلالته على العقاب الحتمي. ويستعرض المفسر السني فخر الدين الرازي القوة البلاغية لتكرار «الإبصار» في خلق التشويق والتحذير. ويتفق التراثان على أن الآية تُقدِّم العزاء للمؤمنين الذين يواجهون الاضطهاد وتُحذِّر الطغاة من المساءلة القادمة. وموضع الاختلاف يكمن في التفصيل والإطار؛ فالعلماء الشيعة يُعمِّقون الجانب الروحي من البصيرة، مُؤكِّدين أنها تتصل بالحكمة التي علَّمها أهل البيت في قراءة الأنماط الإلهية في التاريخ، ويمدُّون المبدأ ليشمل التبرئة الأخيرة للأئمة الذين مثل خصومهم جميعاً أمام الهزيمة أو الخزي في نهاية المطاف. في حين يقصر المفسرون السنة الآية في الغالب على السياق التاريخي الأصلي لقريش التي لاقت هزيمتها في بدر ومكة. غير أن التراثين يتفقان على أن الآية تُقرِّر جلاء العدل الإلهي في نهاية المطاف، مما يجعل آلام الأبرار في الحاضر مؤقتة وانتصار الظالم الزائل وهماً عابراً.
175.layer1: Verse 175 concludes this passage with a powerful divine instruction: 'And watch them — and they will soon see.' The Arabic 'wa absirhum' (watch them) and 'fa-sawfa yubsirun' (they shall soon see) create a striking contrast between the composed observation of the Prophet and the rude awakening awaiting the disbelievers. Allah tells the Prophet to calmly watch what will befall his opponents, while those same opponents will soon be made to see the consequences of their rejection and arrogance. The word 'sawfa' carries a sense of certainty about a near future event — it is not 'perhaps' but 'it will surely happen, and soon.' This verse mirrors verse 175's companion verse 179 later in the same surah, forming a literary bracket that underscores the theme. For the persecuted believers of Mecca, this was a statement of divine justice — their tormentors who mocked them and harmed them would one day see clearly who was on the right side. The verse also carries a psychological benefit for the believer: rather than seeking personal revenge or becoming consumed by anger at injustice, the believer is called to a composed watchfulness, knowing that Allah's justice is certain and that He handles the ultimate accounting. This models a spiritually healthy response to persecution — not bitterness or obsession with retribution, but a calm, dignified certainty that the truth will manifest. The verse teaches that one of the highest forms of patience is the ability to witness wrongdoing without being destroyed by it, trusting entirely in divine justice.
175.layer2: Ibn Kathir explains verse 175 as meaning: 'Watch them and see what will happen to them by way of punishment for their opposition toward you and their disbelief in you.' He notes that 'absirhum' is a divine command to the Prophet to simply observe — an instruction that communicates divine control over the unfolding of events. Ibn Kathir connects this verse to the historical outcome: the Meccan leaders who most fiercely persecuted the Muslims — Abu Jahl, Abu Lahab, and others — met their ends within years of this revelation. Abu Jahl was killed at Badr, Abu Lahab died shortly after the battle, and the city of Mecca itself surrendered to the Prophet whom it had expelled. This historical fulfilment, Ibn Kathir argues, is the tafsir bil-waqi (interpretation by reality) of verse 175. Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan notes that some scholars of the Salaf read 'absirhum' as meaning 'wait and observe with patience,' reinforcing the thematic connection with verse 174's command to turn away temporarily. The pairing of 'watch them' with 'they shall see' creates what classical Arabic rhetoric calls a muqabala (an antithetical parallelism), where the Prophet's calm, knowing observation is set against the disbelievers' coming shock of realisation. Imam Qurtubi notes that the verse implicitly addresses the psychology of the believer: it prevents him from despairing or becoming impatient by reminding him that Allah observes all and will deal with injustice in His own time and manner. This is connected to the Quranic principle that Allah does not allow any deed, good or evil, to go unaccounted.
175.layer3: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran finds verse 175 to be one of the most emotionally powerful expressions in the surah. He writes that the divine command 'watch them' places the Prophet — and by extension all believers — in a position of spiritual superiority. They observe with certainty and serenity while the disbelievers rush toward their own reckoning. Qutb sees in this verse the Quranic logic of history: those who deny truth are not ultimately in control of their narrative, and their apparent dominance is temporary. The phrase 'fa-sawfa yubsirun' (they shall soon see) is, for Qutb, a divine promise of moral clarity — the disbelievers will one day have the veil lifted and see the reality they refused to acknowledge. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir draws attention to the rhetorical symmetry between verse 175 and verse 179 of the same surah, noting that the repetition of this phrase creates a literary and thematic closure (ring composition) for the entire passage, emphasising the certainty and comprehensiveness of the divine promise. Sheikh Muhammad al-Sha'rawi reflected on this verse as a model for how believers should relate to injustice in the world — with patient vigilance rather than reckless reaction, trusting that Allah's court of justice never closes and never misses a case. Contemporary scholars apply verse 175 to the lived experience of Muslim communities who witness oppression: the Quranic response is neither passive resignation nor vengeful anger, but a composed watchfulness grounded in the unshakeable certainty that divine justice will manifest, as it always has, in ways and at times that only Allah determines.

concepts.title: Mocking Challenge
concepts.coreInsight: The disbelievers mockingly challenged the Prophet to bring Allah's punishment, revealing their arrogance.
concepts.whyItMatters: Mocking divine warnings is a sign of spiritual blindness that precedes sudden calamity.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: کافروں نے مذاق میں نبی کو چیلنج کیا کہ اللہ کا عذاب لائیں، اپنے تکبر کو ظاہر کرتے ہوئے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: الہی انتباہات کا مذاق اڑانا روحانی اندھے پن کی علامت ہے جو اچانک آفت سے پہلے آتی ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تحدى الكافرون النبي ساخرين أن يأتي بعذاب الله، كاشفين عن غطرستهم.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: السخرية من التحذيرات الإلهية علامة على العمى الروحي الذي يسبق الكارثة المفاجئة.

concepts.title: Divine Mercy Delay
concepts.coreInsight: Allah's delay in punishment is mercy, giving people time to repent, not a sign of weakness.
concepts.whyItMatters: Every moment before divine punishment is an opportunity for repentance; delay is grace, not absence.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: عذاب میں اللہ کی تاخیر رحمت ہے، لوگوں کو توبہ کرنے کا وقت دیتے ہوئے، کمزوری کی علامت نہیں۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: الہی عذاب سے پہلے ہر لمحہ توبہ کا موقع ہے؛ تاخیر فضل ہے، غیر موجودگی نہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تأخير الله في العقاب رحمة، يعطي الناس وقتًا للتوبة، وليس علامة ضعف.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: كل لحظة قبل العقاب الإلهي فرصة للتوبة؛ التأخير نعمة وليس غياب.

concepts.title: Rhetorical Warning
concepts.coreInsight: The rhetorical question format intensifies the warning - their impatience will lead to regret.
concepts.whyItMatters: Allah's rhetorical questions aren't seeking information but emphasizing the gravity of our choices.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: بیانیہ سوال کی شکل انتباہ کو تیز کرتی ہے - ان کی بے صبری افسوس کا باعث بنے گی۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ کے بیانیہ سوالات معلومات طلب نہیں کر رہے بلکہ ہماری پسند کی اہمیت پر زور دے رہے ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يكثف شكل السؤال البلاغي التحذير - سيؤدي نفاد صبرهم إلى الندم.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: أسئلة الله البلاغية لا تسعى للمعلومات بل تؤكد على خطورة خياراتنا.

176.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree on the interpretation of this verse as exposing the foolishness of the Quraysh who mockingly challenged the Prophet to bring divine punishment. Ibn Kathir provides examples of such challenges, including Abu Jahl's statement asking Allah to destroy him with stones if the Quran was true. Al-Tabari explains that this verse exposes their arrogance and disbelief. Al-Qurtubi notes that challenging divine punishment is the height of ignorance and spiritual blindness. There is consensus across both traditions that such mockery demonstrates hardness of heart and distance from faith. Sunni exegete Fakhr al-Din al-Razi discusses the rhetorical power of framing this as a question—it emphasizes the absurdity of their position. Both traditions agree that this verse warns against treating divine warnings lightly and shows that mockery of truth leads to destruction. Where slight differences appear is in theological development: Shia scholars tend to emphasize the concept of istidraj (gradual leading to destruction) more explicitly, explaining that people's arrogance increases until they mock the very thing that will destroy them, which is itself a form of divine punishment. Sunni commentators focus more on the immediate historical context without necessarily developing a systematic concept. However, both agree that the verse serves as a warning that divine punishment is real and serious, not a matter for jokes, and that those who mock it will face devastating consequences that transform their mockery into regret.
176.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی علماء دونوں اس آیت کی تشریح پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ قریش کی حماقت کو بے نقاب کرتی ہے جنہوں نے مذاق میں نبی کو الہٰی سزا لانے کا چیلنج کیا۔ ابن کثیر ایسے چیلنجز کی مثالیں فراہم کرتے ہیں، بشمول ابوجہل کا بیان کہ اللہ سے کہا کہ اگر قرآن سچ ہے تو اسے پتھروں سے تباہ کر دے۔ طبری وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ یہ آیت ان کے تکبر اور عدم ایمان کو بے نقاب کرتی ہے۔ قرطبی نوٹ کرتے ہیں کہ الہٰی سزا کو چیلنج کرنا جہالت اور روحانی اندھے پن کی انتہا ہے۔ دونوں روایات میں اتفاق ہے کہ ایسا مذاق دل کی سختی اور ایمان سے دوری کو ظاہر کرتا ہے۔ سنی مفسر فخر الدین رازی اس کے سوال کے طور پر بنانے کی بلاغتی طاقت پر بحث کرتے ہیں، ان کی پوزیشن کی بیہودگی پر زور دیتے ہوئے۔ دونوں روایات متفق ہیں کہ یہ آیت الہٰی انتباہات کو ہلکا لینے کے خلاف خبردار کرتی ہے۔
176.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على تفسير هذه الآية بأنها تفضح حماقة قريش التي استعجلت العذاب الإلهي في صورة تحدٍّ ساخر للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. فابن كثير في تفسيره يستشهد بمواقف كمقولة أبي جهل الذي طلب من الله أن يُمطر عليهم الحجارة إن كان القرآن حقاً. والطبري في جامع البيان يُبيِّن أن هذه الآية تكشف غطرستهم وكفرهم. والقرطبي يُلاحِظ أن تحدِّي العذاب الإلهي يمثِّل ذروة الجهل والعمى الروحي. وثمة إجماع في التراثين على أن هذا الاستهزاء يدل على قسوة القلب والبُعد عن الإيمان. ويتناول فخر الدين الرازي في تفسيره الواسع القوة البلاغية لصياغة الآية سؤالاً استنكارياً، مُبيِّناً أنها تُضخِّم سخافة موقفهم. ويتَّفق التراثان على أن الآية تُحذِّر من الاستهانة بالإنذارات الإلهية، وتُريَنا أن السخرية من الحق تُفضي إلى الهلاك. أما الفارق الدقيق في التطوير النظري فيكمن في أن العلماء الشيعة يُشدِّدون على مفهوم الاستدراج بصورة أكثر وضوحاً، إذ يُفسِّرون أن أنانية الإنسان وتكبُّره تتعاظم حتى يستهزئ بالشيء الذي سيُرديه وهو نفسه نوع من العذاب. أما المفسِّرون السنة فيُركِّزون أكثر على السياق التاريخي الآني. بيد أن التراثين يتَّفقان على أن الآية إنذار بأن عذاب الله حقيقة جسيمة لا مجال فيها للهزل، وأن من استهزؤوا به سيعيش استهزاؤهم تحوُّلاً إلى ندم لا تنفع معه التوبة.
176.layer1: Verse 176 of Surah As-Saffat presents a rhetorical question from Allah directed at those who mockingly challenge the divine punishment: 'Do they seek to hasten Our punishment?' This question carries a tone of reproach and warning. The Meccan disbelievers who rejected the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) were not merely indifferent to the warnings they received — they actively taunted the believers and mocked the idea that any punishment from Allah would come. Their attitude was one of arrogant defiance, as if daring Allah to act. This verse is a divine corrective: Allah is asking whether they truly comprehend what they are inviting. It is a rhetorical device intended to shake their complacency and expose the absurdity and danger of their position. In practical terms, this verse teaches Muslims that heedlessness toward divine warnings is not a sign of strength but of profound foolishness. The key Arabic verb 'yasta'jilun' means 'they seek to hasten' or 'they demand urgently,' conveying active impatience rather than passive disbelief. The verse calls believers to reflect on the mercy inherent in divine delay — Allah's withholding of punishment is itself an act of grace, giving people time to return to the truth. This verse was revealed in a context where the Quraysh pagans would sarcastically demand to see the punishment the Prophet warned them of, as if challenging the credibility of the message. Rather than responding with immediate punishment, Allah uses this verse to counsel patience and warn of consequences to come.
176.layer2: Imam Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan records that this verse continues the overarching theme of divine sovereignty and the fate of those who rejected the messengers throughout history. The rhetorical question — 'afabi-adhabhina yasta'jilun' — is interpreted by Tabari as an expression of divine astonishment at human audacity and heedlessness. The disbelievers of Mecca, like those before them, openly mocked the Prophet (peace be upon him) and sarcastically called for the punishment they were threatened with. Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim explains that this verse serves as a sharp rebuke: these people, out of their denial and mockery, were actually calling for the torment that would seal their fate. The phrasing is consistent with other Meccan revelations where the polytheists demanded signs and punishment as if testing the Prophet's claims. Ibn Kathir draws on earlier narrations that show the Quraysh would taunt believers with phrases like 'When will this punishment come, if you are telling the truth?' Allah's answer here is both a warning and a display of forbearance. The scholars of the Salaf understood this verse within the broader narrative of divine justice: the delay in punishment is not a sign of divine inability or neglect, but an extension of mercy. The word 'adhab' (punishment) here refers to both worldly chastisement — which would eventually come through the battles of Badr and the conquest of Makkah — and the ultimate punishment of the Hereafter. Imam Qurtubi adds that this verse implicitly praises the believers who remain patient in the face of the disbelievers' mockery.
176.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir places this verse within the concluding rhetorical section of Surah As-Saffat, noting that verses 176 through 182 form a unified closing movement that shifts tone from narrative to direct divine address. The rhetorical question of verse 176 is, in al-Zuhayli's reading, a form of divine scorn — not born of anger alone, but of the profound irony that those who are being warned persist in their self-destructive defiance. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describes this moment as one of cosmic drama: the Creator addressing the creation that has turned against its own salvation. Qutb emphasizes the literary power of the question — it does not need an answer because the question itself is the answer, exposing the tragic foolishness of those who mistake divine patience for weakness. From a contemporary perspective, this verse resonates in contexts where people dismiss religious warnings as irrelevant or antiquated, or where cynicism masquerades as rational inquiry. The verse reminds the believer that the seriousness of accountability does not diminish because it is delayed. Muhammad al-Sharawis commentary highlights that 'yasta'jilun' in the present tense indicates ongoing, habitual behavior — these were not isolated provocations but a persistent pattern of mockery. This has direct relevance today: believers should not be destabilized by the scoffing of those who reject faith, understanding that Allah's timing is precise and His forbearance is purposeful. The verse ultimately grounds the Muslim's confidence in divine justice even when it is not immediately visible.

concepts.title: Sudden Descent
concepts.coreInsight: When divine punishment finally arrives, it comes suddenly to their very homes (sahatihim - their courtyard).
concepts.whyItMatters: Divine warnings may seem distant until punishment arrives at your doorstep; preparation can't wait.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: جب الہی عذاب آخر کار آتا ہے، تو یہ اچانک ان کے گھروں تک (ساحتہم - ان کے صحن) میں آتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: الہی انتباہات دور معلوم ہو سکتے ہیں جب تک کہ عذاب آپ کے دروازے پر نہ آ جائے؛ تیاری انتظار نہیں کر سکتی۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: عندما ينزل العقاب الإلهي أخيرًا، يأتي فجأة إلى منازلهم ذاتها (بساحتهم - فنائهم).
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: قد تبدو التحذيرات الإلهية بعيدة حتى ينزل العقاب على عتبة بابك؛ الاستعداد لا يمكن أن ينتظر.

concepts.title: Evil Morning
concepts.coreInsight: The metaphor of an 'evil morning' (sa'a sabah) conveys awakening to irreversible calamity instead of hope.
concepts.whyItMatters: What we mock today may become tomorrow's nightmare; heed warnings before the dawn of regret.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: 'بری صبح' (سا صباح) کا استعارہ امید کی بجائے ناقابل واپسی آفت کی بیداری کو بیان کرتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: جس کا ہم آج مذاق اڑاتے ہیں وہ کل کا خواب خراب بن سکتا ہے؛ افسوس کی صبح سے پہلے انتباہات پر دھیان دیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تنقل استعارة 'الصباح السيئ' (فساء صباح) الاستيقاظ على كارثة لا رجعة فيها بدلاً من الأمل.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: ما نسخر منه اليوم قد يصبح كابوس الغد؛ انتبه للتحذيرات قبل فجر الندم.

concepts.title: The Warned Ones
concepts.coreInsight: They're called 'al-mundharin' (those who were warned) - emphasizing they had advance notice but ignored it.
concepts.whyItMatters: Punishment is most severe for those who were warned; ignorance isn't an excuse when prophets came.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: انہیں 'المنذرین' (جن کو متنبہ کیا گیا) کہا جاتا ہے - زور دیتے ہوئے کہ انہیں پیشگی اطلاع تھی لیکن انہوں نے نظرانداز کیا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ان لوگوں کے لیے سزا سب سے سخت ہے جن کو متنبہ کیا گیا؛ نبیوں کے آنے کے بعد جہالت کوئی عذر نہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يُطلق عليهم 'المنذرين' - مؤكدًا أنهم تلقوا إشعارًا مسبقًا لكنهم تجاهلوه.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: العقاب أشد للذين حُذروا؛ الجهل ليس عذرًا عندما جاء الأنبياء.

177.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree on the interpretation of this verse as describing the devastating punishment that will befall those who were warned but persisted in rejection. Ibn Kathir explains that this refers to the punishment descending upon the Quraysh at Badr and other battles, and ultimately to the Day of Judgment. Al-Tabari provides similar interpretation, noting that 'sahati-him' (their territory) indicates the punishment will strike them in their homeland. Al-Qurtubi emphasizes that 'muntharin' (those who were warned) shows they have no excuse—they were clearly notified. Sunni exegete Fakhr al-Din al-Razi discusses the powerful imagery of 'evil morning,' noting that morning usually brings relief and hope, but for these people it brings disaster. There is consensus across both traditions that this verse was historically fulfilled at Badr and will be ultimately fulfilled on the Day of Judgment. Both agree that the verse serves as a warning to take divine admonitions seriously. Minor differences appear in extended application: Shia scholars tend to emphasize the pattern of this principle applying to all oppressors throughout history, including those who opposed the Ahlul Bayt, citing examples like the fall of the Umayyad dynasty or the defeat of those who killed Imam Husayn. Sunni commentators focus more specifically on the original Quraysh context. However, both traditions agree that the core lesson is universal: those who receive clear warnings but persist in rejection will face sudden, terrible consequences that transform their mockery into eternal regret.
177.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی علماء دونوں اس آیت کی تشریح پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ تباہ کن سزا کو بیان کرتی ہے جو ان لوگوں پر آئے گی جنہیں خبردار کیا گیا لیکن مسترد میں جاری رہے۔ ابن کثیر وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ یہ قریش پر جنگ بدر اور دیگر جنگوں میں اترنے والی سزا کی طرف اشارہ کرتی ہے، اور بالآخر قیامت کے دن۔ طبری اسی طرح کی تشریح فراہم کرتے ہیں، نوٹ کرتے ہوئے کہ 'ساحَتِہِم' (ان کا علاقہ) ظاہر کرتا ہے کہ سزا ان کی سرزمین میں انہیں ماریگی۔ قرطبی زور دیتے ہیں کہ 'مُنذَرِیْن' (خبردار کیے گئے) ظاہر کرتا ہے کہ ان کے پاس کوئی عذر نہیں، انہیں واضح طور پر مطلع کیا گیا تھا۔ سنی مفسر فخر الدین رازی 'بری صبح' کی طاقتور منظرکشی پر بحث کرتے ہیں، نوٹ کرتے ہوئے کہ صبح عام طور پر راحت اور امید لاتی ہے، لیکن ان لوگوں کے لیے تباہی لاتی ہے۔ دونوں روایات میں اتفاق ہے کہ یہ آیت تاریخی طور پر بدر میں پوری ہوئی اور بالآخر قیامت کے دن پوری ہوگی۔
177.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على تفسير هذه الآية بوصفها تصويراً للعقوبة المُدمِّرة التي ستُصيب من أُنذروا وأصرُّوا على الرفض. فابن كثير يُفسِّر الآية بأنها تُشير إلى العقوبة التي حلَّت بقريش في بدر وغيره من الغزوات، وإلى يوم القيامة في المآل. والطبري يُقدِّم تفسيراً مماثلاً مُنبِّهاً إلى أن «سَاحَتِهِمْ» تدل على أن العقوبة ستضرب في عقر ديارهم. والقرطبي يُؤكِّد أن «الْمُنذَرِين» يُلغي العذر ويُثبت المسؤولية. وفخر الدين الرازي يتأمَّل الصورة البلاغية لـ«سَاءَ صَبَاحُ» مُلاحِظاً أن الصباح يُرمز عادةً للراحة والأمل، غير أنه لهؤلاء يتحوَّل إلى وخز الكارثة. وثمة إجماع في التراثين على أن الآية تحقَّقت تاريخياً في بدر وستتحقَّق تحقُّقاً كاملاً يوم القيامة. وكلاهما يتَّفق على أن الدرس الجوهري عالمي: من تلقَّوا الإنذارات البيِّنة وأصرُّوا على الرفض سيواجهون عواقب مباغتة فادحة تُحوِّل استهزاءهم إلى ندم أبدي. والفارق الطفيف في الامتداد هو أن العلماء الشيعة يُشدِّدون على انطباق هذا المبدأ على سائر الظالمين عبر التاريخ بما فيهم من عادوا أهل البيت عليهم السلام، مستشهدين بسقوط الدولة الأموية وهلاك قتلة الإمام الحسين عليه السلام. أما المفسِّرون السنة فيُركِّزون أكثر على سياق قريش. غير أن التراثين يتَّفقان على الجوهر: أن هذه الآية عظة بالغة بأن إنذارات الله حقيقة لا محيد عنها.
177.layer1: Verse 177 answers the implicit question of verse 176 with a vivid and sobering reply: 'But when it descends in their courtyard, evil will be the morning for those who had been warned.' Having asked whether the disbelievers truly wish to hasten the punishment, Allah now describes what will happen when that punishment actually arrives. The phrase 'in their courtyard' — or 'in their space, their territory' — suggests an intimacy of destruction: this is not a distant punishment but one that will arrive at their very doorstep, inescapable and immediate. The word 'fasa'a' — meaning 'how evil' or 'how terrible' — is an expression of deep condemnation and horror. The phrase 'sabahu al-mundhirin' — 'the morning of those who were warned' — is particularly striking. Morning is typically a time of hope and fresh beginning, but here it becomes the moment of devastating reckoning. This points to the morning of the Battle of Badr, where the Quraysh faced sudden and catastrophic defeat after years of rejecting the Prophet's message. It also carries a broader eschatological meaning pointing to the morning of judgment. The key lesson for Muslims is that warnings from Allah through His prophets are not threats to be dismissed but merciful reminders. To reject them is to choose the very fate being described. This verse also highlights the fulfillment of prophecy — what was predicted came to pass precisely as described, affirming the truth of the Quran and the Prophet's mission.
177.layer2: In Jami al-Bayan, Imam Tabari records multiple narrations explaining the phrase 'when it descends in their courtyard.' As-Suddi and other early commentators understood 'their courtyard' to mean their dwellings and places of gathering — the punishment would come to them in their own spaces, leaving no room for escape. Tabari notes that this was understood by the Companions and their successors as a reference to the worldly punishment that befell the Quraysh through the battles they lost, particularly Badr, where prominent leaders of Makkah were killed and their pride destroyed. Ibn Kathir builds on this in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, connecting this verse to the earlier divine promise in the surah that the armies of Allah would be victorious. He emphasizes the term 'fa-sa'a sabahu l-mundhirin' — 'how evil will be the morning of those who were warned' — as a literary expression of severe condemnation, noting that the morning of Badr was indeed a catastrophic morning for those who had rejected the Prophet. The scholars of tafsir understand 'morning' here as both literal — Badr was fought in the morning hours — and symbolic, representing the moment when all of the disbelievers' assumptions were shattered. Imam Qurtubi notes the grammatical construction emphasizes the certainty and completeness of the punishment. The conditional 'when it descends' (idha nazala) rather than 'if it descends' indicates its inevitability. This verse thus stands as a testimony to the truthfulness of divine promise and the precision of prophetic warning.
177.layer3: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reflects deeply on the phrase 'evil will be the morning of those who were warned,' noting the heartbreaking paradox: the morning was supposed to be when they saw the truth vindicated, but instead it becomes the morning of their own destruction. Qutb views this as one of the Quran's most powerful rhetorical devices — allowing the punishment to be described from within the perspective of its victims, as they experience the full weight of what they once mockingly denied. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir notes that this verse completes the logical arc begun in verse 176: those who hastened punishment will receive it, but not on their terms — it will arrive when Allah decrees, in the manner Allah chooses, and with the finality Allah intends. Contemporary Muslim scholars draw from this verse a powerful lesson about the nature of divine forbearance. Allah's delay in punishment should not be interpreted as permission to continue in wrongdoing. When the punishment comes, it is total and irreversible. Ibn Uthaymeen's broader exegetical framework, applied to this verse, emphasizes that the Quran frequently uses historical punishments as mirrors for the present generation — reminding readers that the divine law of consequence is still operative. The verse also carries a reminder for the Muslim community: the believers who were warned alongside the disbelievers but heeded the warning are saved from this terrible morning. Accepting prophetic guidance is the only protection against being among 'those who were warned' but did not listen.

concepts.title: Repeated Command
concepts.coreInsight: This verse repeats verse 174 word-for-word, emphasizing the instruction through divine repetition.
concepts.whyItMatters: When Allah repeats a command, it signals critical importance and requires extra attention and obedience.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: یہ آیت آیت 174 کو لفظ بہ لفظ دہراتی ہے، الہی تکرار کے ذریعے ہدایت پر زور دیتے ہوئے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: جب اللہ کسی حکم کو دہراتا ہے، تو یہ اہم اہمیت کی علامت ہے اور اضافی توجہ اور اطاعت کی ضرورت ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تكرر هذه الآية الآية 174 حرفيًا، مؤكدة التعليمات من خلال التكرار الإلهي.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: عندما يكرر الله أمرًا، فإنه يشير إلى أهمية حاسمة ويتطلب اهتمامًا وطاعة إضافيين.

concepts.title: Reinforced Patience
concepts.coreInsight: Repeating the command to turn away reinforces that patience with opposition is central to prophetic mission.
concepts.whyItMatters: The repetition teaches us that patience isn't passive resignation but active obedience to divine strategy.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: منہ موڑنے کے حکم کو دہرانا تقویت دیتا ہے کہ مخالفت کے ساتھ صبر نبوی مشن کا مرکزی حصہ ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: تکرار ہمیں سکھاتی ہے کہ صبر غیر فعال استعفیٰ نہیں بلکہ الہی حکمت عملی کی فعال اطاعت ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يعزز تكرار الأمر بالابتعاد أن الصبر مع المعارضة محوري للبعثة النبوية.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: يعلمنا التكرار أن الصبر ليس استسلامًا سلبيًا بل طاعة نشطة للاستراتيجية الإلهية.

concepts.title: Literary Emphasis
concepts.coreInsight: The Quran's literary technique of repetition creates emphasis and aids memorization of key concepts.
concepts.whyItMatters: Divine rhetoric isn't redundant; repetition serves pedagogical and spiritual purposes in revelation.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: قرآن کی تکرار کی ادبی تکنیک زور پیدا کرتی ہے اور کلیدی تصورات کو یاد کرنے میں مدد کرتی ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: الہی بیان زائد نہیں؛ تکرار وحی میں تعلیمی اور روحانی مقاصد کی خدمت کرتی ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: تخلق تقنية القرآن الأدبية للتكرار تأكيدًا وتساعد في حفظ المفاهيم الرئيسية.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: البلاغة الإلهية ليست زائدة؛ التكرار يخدم أغراضًا تربوية وروحية في الوحي.

178.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree on the interpretation of this verse as repeating the command for strategic patience and disengagement from direct confrontation. Ibn Kathir explains that the repetition emphasizes the importance of the instruction and provides additional comfort to the Prophet. Al-Tabari notes that some scholars interpret each instance of the command as referring to different times or circumstances, while others see it as simple emphasis. Al-Qurtubi emphasizes that the repetition teaches that patience with oppressors is difficult and requires repeated reinforcement. Sunni exegete Fakhr al-Din al-Razi discusses various interpretations of why the verse is repeated, including that it creates rhetorical rhythm and emphasis. There is consensus across both traditions that the verse provided psychological comfort and strategic guidance to the Prophet during persecution. Where traditions differ slightly is in extended doctrinal application: Shia scholars use this and similar verses as scriptural foundation for the principle of taqiyyah (precautionary dissimulation) practiced by the Imams when facing overwhelming oppression, arguing that strategic disengagement when necessary is established by Quranic command. Most Sunni scholars acknowledge the historical context of strategic patience without developing it into a systematic doctrine. However, both traditions agree that the verse teaches wisdom in choosing when to confront and when to wait, trusting in divine timing rather than forcing confrontations that would be strategically unwise or destructive to the community's interests.
178.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی علماء دونوں اس آیت کی تشریح پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ حکمت عملی کے صبر اور براہ راست مقابلے سے الگ ہونے کے حکم کو دہراتی ہے۔ ابن کثیر وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ اعادہ پیغام کی یقینی نوعیت اور اہمیت پر زور دیتا ہے اور نبی کو مسلسل سکون فراہم کرتا ہے۔ طبری نوٹ کرتے ہیں کہ کچھ علماء ہر حکم کی مثال کو مختلف اوقات یا حالات کی طرف اشارہ کرنے کے طور پر تشریح کرتے ہیں، جبکہ دوسرے اسے سادہ زور کے طور پر دیکھتے ہیں۔ قرطبی زور دیتے ہیں کہ اعادہ سکھاتا ہے کہ ظالموں کے ساتھ صبر مشکل ہے اور بار بار تقویت کی ضرورت ہے۔ سنی مفسر فخر الدین رازی آیت کے دہرائے جانے کی مختلف تشریحات پر بحث کرتے ہیں، بشمول یہ کہ یہ بلاغتی تال اور زور بناتا ہے۔ دونوں روایات میں اتفاق ہے کہ آیت نے ظلم کے دوران نبی کو نفسیاتی سکون اور حکمت عملی کی رہنمائی فراہم کی۔
178.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على تفسير هذه الآية بوصفها تكراراً للأمر بالصبر الاستراتيجي والابتعاد عن المواجهة المباشرة. فابن كثير يُفسِّر أن التكرار يُؤكِّد أهمية التعليمة ويُضاعف الطمأنينة للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. والطبري يُشير إلى أن بعض العلماء يُفسِّر كل حالة من حالتَي الأمر على أنها تُشير إلى وقت أو ظرف مختلف، فيما يرى آخرون أنها مجرَّد تأكيد. والقرطبي يُشدِّد على أن الصبر مع الظالمين صعب المِراس يستدعي تعزيزاً متكرِّراً. وفخر الدين الرازي يُناقش وجوه توجيه التكرار ومنها أنه يُنشئ إيقاعاً وأثراً بلاغياً. وثمة إجماع في التراثين على أن الآية أتاحت للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم الراحة النفسية والإرشاد الاستراتيجي في محنة الاضطهاد. والفارق الطفيف في الامتداد العقدي هو أن العلماء الشيعة يستنِدون إلى هذه الآية ونظائرها دليلاً قرآنياً على مبدأ التقية الذي مارسه الأئمة عند مواجهة الغَلَبة القاهرة، مُقرِّرين أن الانسحاب الاستراتيجي عند الحاجة أمر مستند إلى الكتاب العزيز. أما أكثر علماء السنة فيُسلِّمون بالسياق التاريخي للصبر دون أن يُطوِّروه مذهباً منهجياً. غير أن التراثين يتَّفقان على أن الآية تُعلِّم حكمة التمييز بين وقت الإقدام ووقت الانتظار، وعلى الثقة بتوقيت الله بدلاً من اصطناع مواجهات تُضرُّ بالجماعة وتُعجِّل بنكبتها.
178.layer1: Verse 178 is a direct divine command to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him): 'And turn away from them for a while.' After describing the terrible fate awaiting those who reject the message, Allah now consoles and instructs His Prophet. This command — 'watawalla' — means to turn away, to step back, to disengage temporarily. It is not a command to abandon the mission but a counsel of patience and composure. The Prophet (peace be upon him) was deeply grieved by the rejection of his people. He longed for them to accept guidance and was pained by their mockery. This verse offers him spiritual relief: do not be consumed by their rejection; remove yourself emotionally from their hostility for a time. The phrase 'for a while' ('hatta hin') implies that the situation is temporary. The period of humiliation and rejection the believers experienced in Mecca was divinely appointed, not permanent. This verse is thus both a command and a promise — Allah is telling the Prophet that this phase will pass. For Muslim readers, this verse is deeply instructive about how to handle opposition, rejection, and hostility. One does not need to engage every attack or respond to every taunt. There is wisdom in stepping back, preserving one's energy and spirit, and trusting Allah's plan to unfold. The key Arabic term 'watawalla' also implies a graceful turning — not a retreat in defeat but a dignified disengagement rooted in trust in Allah.
178.layer2: Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim explains that this command — 'watawalla anhum hatta hin' — is a divine instruction to the Prophet to bear with patience the harm and mockery of his enemies, knowing that a specific term has been appointed by Allah. Ibn Kathir links this verse to other Meccan revelations where the Prophet is counseled to persevere through difficulty and wait for Allah's decree. He notes that 'hin' — meaning 'a time' or 'a season' — was fulfilled with the permission to emigrate to Medina and subsequently the military victories that followed, particularly Badr and later the conquest of Makkah. Tabari in Jami al-Bayan presents the opinion that this verse was specifically a comfort to the Prophet during the harshest years of the Meccan period, when the Quraysh intensified their persecution. The command to 'turn away' does not mean abandoning the call to truth but rather ceasing to be broken by those who will not listen, instead placing the matter in Allah's hands. Imam Qurtubi explores the fiqhi dimension of this verse in discussing how it relates to the concept of patience (sabr) in Islamic ethics. He notes that scholars of the Salaf understood this verse as one of those passages later 'strengthened' or contextually clarified by the verses of fighting (qital), which were revealed in Medina — meaning the period of graceful withdrawal eventually gave way to a mandate of active defense. The verse thus captures a precise moment in the progression of prophetic strategy under divine guidance.
178.layer3: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir frames verse 178 as a lesson in prophetic wisdom and divine pedagogy. The Prophet (peace be upon him) was not simply told to 'ignore' the disbelievers — he was told to disengage with dignity and purpose, knowing that divine intervention would come in its proper time. This reflects the Islamic principle that human effort and divine timing must align: believers do their work faithfully, and then trust Allah to bring events to their proper conclusion. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran sees in this verse a profound spiritual teaching about not being emotionally enslaved to the reactions of others. The Prophet's distress over the rejection of the Quraysh was genuine and compassionate, yet Allah guides him toward an inner freedom — an emotional and spiritual independence from the approval or acknowledgment of those who would not listen. This teaching is remarkably relevant in the contemporary context of dawah (invitation to Islam) and interfaith engagement. Callers to Islam often face mockery, dismissal, and hostility. This verse gives them prophetic precedent for gracefully stepping back rather than descending into endless argument. Muhammad al-Sharawis reading emphasizes the mercy embedded in this verse — it shows that Allah never leaves His Prophet alone in distress but always provides guidance, comfort, and a pathway forward. The 'hatta hin' — 'for a while' — is itself a divine guarantee that the difficulty is bounded and that relief is coming, a principle that applies to all believers in times of trial.

concepts.title: Parallel Repetition
concepts.coreInsight: This verse parallels verse 175, creating a symmetric structure that emphasizes witnessing divine justice.
concepts.whyItMatters: The Quran's structural symmetry reinforces its message; form and meaning work together in revelation.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: یہ آیت آیت 175 کے متوازی ہے، ایک ہم آہنگ ڈھانچہ بناتے ہوئے جو الہی انصاف کے گواہ ہونے پر زور دیتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: قرآن کی ساختی ہم آہنگی اس کے پیغام کو تقویت دیتی ہے؛ شکل اور معنی وحی میں مل کر کام کرتے ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: توازي هذه الآية الآية 175، مخلقة بنية متماثلة تؤكد على الشهادة على العدالة الإلهية.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: يعزز التماثل الهيكلي للقرآن رسالته؛ الشكل والمعنى يعملان معًا في الوحي.

concepts.title: Double Assurance
concepts.coreInsight: Repeating the seeing motif doubles the assurance that truth will be manifested to all.
concepts.whyItMatters: Allah's double promise removes all doubt; both believers and disbelievers will witness the outcome.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: دیکھنے کے موضوع کو دہرانا یقین کو دوگنا کرتا ہے کہ حق سب کے لیے ظاہر ہوگا۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ کا دوہرا وعدہ تمام شک کو دور کرتا ہے؛ مومن اور کافر دونوں نتیجہ دیکھیں گے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يضاعف تكرار موضوع الرؤية التأكيد على أن الحق سيتجلى للجميع.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: وعد الله المزدوج يزيل كل شك؛ سيشهد المؤمنون والكافرون النتيجة.

concepts.title: Shortened Form
concepts.coreInsight: The command is shorter ('absir' instead of 'absirhum'), intensifying it to a universal call to witness.
concepts.whyItMatters: Sometimes divine commands become more intense through brevity; less words can mean more urgency.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: حکم مختصر ہے ('ابصر' بجائے 'ابصرہم')، اسے ایک آفاقی گواہی کی پکار کی طرف تیز کرتے ہوئے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: بعض اوقات الہی احکام اختصار کے ذریعے زیادہ تیز ہو جاتے ہیں؛ کم الفاظ کا مطلب زیادہ فوریت ہو سکتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: الأمر أقصر ('أبصر' بدلاً من 'أبصرهم')، مكثفًا إياه إلى دعوة عالمية للشهادة.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: أحيانًا تصبح الأوامر الإلهية أكثر كثافة من خلال الإيجاز؛ كلمات أقل يمكن أن تعني إلحاحًا أكبر.

179.layer4: Both Shia and Sunni scholars agree on the interpretation of this verse as repeating the command to observe and the promise that rejecters will face consequences. Ibn Kathir explains that the repetition emphasizes the certainty and importance of the message. Al-Tabari notes that this creates rhetorical emphasis and provides continued comfort to the Prophet. Al-Qurtubi emphasizes that both the command to observe and the promise of their witnessing punishment are stressed through repetition. Sunni exegete Fakhr al-Din al-Razi discusses the rhetorical power of repetition in creating anticipation and emphasis. There is consensus across both traditions that the verse instructs the Prophet to observe divine justice and promises that rejecters will face clear consequences. Both agree that this provides comfort during persecution and teaches patience. Minor differences appear in the depth of emphasis on basira (spiritual insight): Shia scholars tend to develop this concept more extensively, emphasizing that observation should be with spiritual understanding and connecting it to the special insight taught by the Ahlul Bayt. Sunni commentators acknowledge the concept of learning from observation but don't necessarily develop it into a systematic spiritual practice to the same extent. However, both traditions agree that the verse establishes that believers should be patient observers of how divine justice unfolds, trusting that those who reject clear guidance will inevitably face consequences that vindicate truth, and that this observation itself strengthens faith and provides comfort during trials.
179.layer4_urdu: شیعہ اور سنی علماء دونوں اس آیت کی تشریح پر متفق ہیں کہ یہ مشاہدہ کرنے کے حکم اور وعدے کو دہراتی ہے کہ مسترد کرنے والے نتائج کا سامنا کریں گے۔ ابن کثیر وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ اعادہ پیغام کی یقینی نوعیت اور اہمیت پر زور دیتا ہے۔ طبری نوٹ کرتے ہیں کہ یہ بلاغتی زور بناتا ہے اور نبی کو مسلسل سکون فراہم کرتا ہے۔ قرطبی زور دیتے ہیں کہ مشاہدہ کرنے کے حکم اور ان کے سزا کے مشاہدے کے وعدے دونوں کو اعادہ کے ذریعے تاکید دی جاتی ہے۔ سنی مفسر فخر الدین رازی توقع اور زور بنانے میں اعادہ کی بلاغتی طاقت پر بحث کرتے ہیں۔ دونوں روایات میں اتفاق ہے کہ آیت نبی کو ہدایت دیتی ہے کہ الہٰی انصاف کا مشاہدہ کریں اور وعدہ کرتی ہے کہ مسترد کرنے والے واضح نتائج کا سامنا کریں گے۔ دونوں متفق ہیں کہ یہ ظلم کے دوران مومنین کو سکون فراہم کرتا ہے اور سکھاتا ہے کہ صبر سے مشاہدہ کریں۔ معمولی فرق بصیرہ (روحانی بصیرت) کی گہرائی میں ظاہر ہوتا ہے: شیعہ علماء اس تصور کو زیادہ وسیع پیمانے پر تیار کرتے ہیں، زور دیتے ہوئے کہ مشاہدہ روحانی سمجھ کے ساتھ ہونا چاہیے اور اسے اہل بیت کی طرف سے سکھائی گئی خاص بصیرت سے جوڑتے ہیں۔
179.layer4_ar: يتَّفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على تفسير هذه الآية بوصفها تكراراً للأمر بالمراقبة والوعد بأن الرافضين سيواجهون العاقبة. فابن كثير يُفسِّر أن التكرار يُؤكِّد يقين الرسالة وأهميتها. والطبري يُلاحِظ أن ذلك يُوفِّر التطمين المستمر للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم. والقرطبي يُؤكِّد أن كلاً من الأمر بالمراقبة والوعد بأنهم سيشهدون العقوبة يُثبَّتان بالتكرار. وفخر الدين الرازي يُناقش القوة البلاغية للتكرار في إحداث الترقُّب والتشديد. وثمة إجماع في التراثين على أن الآية تأمر النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم بمراقبة العدل الإلهي وتعده بأن الرافضين سيواجهون عواقب واضحة. وكلاهما يرى أن ذلك يُقدِّم عزاءً في محنة الاضطهاد ويُرسِّخ الصبر. والفارق الطفيف في التوسُّع يكمن في مفهوم البصيرة؛ إذ يُميل العلماء الشيعة إلى تعميق هذا المفهوم وتنظيمه، مُشدِّدين على ضرورة أن تكون المراقبة بفهم روحي ومربوطةً بالبصيرة الخاصة التي يُضفيها تعليم أهل البيت عليهم السلام. أما المفسِّرون السنة فيُسلِّمون بأهمية التعلُّم من المراقبة دون أن يُطوِّروها ممارسةً روحية منهجية بالضرورة. غير أن التراثين يتَّفقان على أن الآية تأمر المؤمنين أن يكونوا شهوداً صابرين على مسيرة العدل الإلهي، واثقين أن المتمرِّدين على الهداية الواضحة سيرون في نهاية المطاف العواقب التي تُثبت الحق.
179.layer1: Verse 179 follows directly from verse 178 and continues the counsel to the Prophet: 'And watch, for they will soon see.' This brief but powerful verse is a divine assurance that the Prophet should remain attentive and observant, because the disbelievers will come to witness the consequences of their rejection. The Arabic 'fa-absir' means 'watch' or 'see,' and 'fasayubsirun' means 'they will soon see' — a promise that events will unfold in a way that makes the truth undeniable. There is a beautiful symmetry here: the Prophet is told to 'watch' and then the disbelievers will themselves 'see.' What they will see is the vindication of everything they mocked — the punishment they demanded in sarcasm, the truth they dismissed, the Prophet they belittled. This verse is deeply linked to the fulfillment of historical prophecy. The Battle of Badr, the conquest of Makkah, and the eventual spread of Islam across the world all constitute the 'seeing' that this verse promises. For believers, this verse is a source of immense confidence.
